*The Essential Teachings of Chan Master Foguo Yuanwu Zhenjue*, Volume One, Part One.
Compiled by the Dharma-heir Wenzi for the instruction of Chief Seat Ming of Huazang (Residing at Tianning Monastery in Jiangning Prefecture).
The Patriarchs have shown directly; how could there be such winding paths? It is simply a matter of those who transcend the ordinary; merely upon hearing a mention, they pick it up.
As soon as he rose, he set off. Even for one with clear eyes to look upon him from afar is already a case of being left behind.
An ancient said, "If one presents a single corner and the other three do not follow, I will not grant my approval. Each and every one must raise one and clarify the three;

with an eye for the subtlest nuances and a turning that rolls like a wheel, being open, penetrating, and swift—only then can one be called a true upholder. Have you not seen how Liangsu met Magu? First...
The first time he saw him, Gu came straight into the abbot’s quarters and shut the door. Liang Sui was left in doubt.
When it came to the second time, Gu strode off into the vegetable garden. Liang Sui suddenly attained enlightenment and said to Gu, "Master, do not deceive me."
"If he had not come to see his preceptor, he would have wasted his entire life being deceived by twelve volumes of sutras and treatises.
Seeing him act in this way, one cannot help but feel it is quite effortless. Upon returning, he said to his disciples: 'What you all know, Liang-sui knows entirely;
what Liang-sui knows, you all do not know. One can truly believe that there is something in his sphere of knowledge that cannot be communicated; you all have simply not yet realized it."
Excellent! You may truly be called a lion cub; yet you must become a blade of grass for that family, and only by emerging one level higher than him can you succeed.
When Bodhidharma traveled through Liang and entered Wei, he "fell into the weeds" to seek out people, sitting coldly at Shaolin for nine years amidst deep snow.
He searched among them for one who could answer, but when it came to the final question—"What have you attained?"—the man simply performed three prostrations and stood in his place.

Thereupon, the words "attaining the marrow" were uttered. To this day, those who remain stuck like a woodcutter waiting for a rabbit compete to regard silent prostrations and standing in one's place as the profound essence of attaining the marrow.
Little do they realize that the sword has long since been lost, yet they are still carving at the stump.

Zhao: "How could he have ever dreamed of the Patriarch? If one is a genuine practitioner of the Way in its true essence, one must transcend emotion and leave behind views, possessing a distinct way of life;
one will never make a living in stagnant water. Only then can one inherit the ancestral estate.
Upon reaching this point, you must know that there is a matter handed down from of old—what is called 'skillfully learning from Liu Xiaohui.'"
One must never take its traces as the teacher. Therefore, the ancients said: "A single phrase that hits the mark is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas. Truly so!
When the Dharma King who destroys existence appears in the world, he preaches the Dharma in various ways according to the inclinations of sentient beings; thus one may know what is being taught.
All of these are merely skillful means. They are intended solely to shatter attachments, shatter doubts, and break through the pathways of the view of self.
Since there are no such numerous evil thoughts or evil views, a Buddha need not even appear in the world, let alone preach various dharmas.

After the ancients had attained the essential meaning, they would go to deep mountains to live in thatched huts or stone chambers, cooking their meals in broken-legged cauldrons for ten or twenty years, completely forgetting the ways of the world and forever bidding farewell to the mundane realm. In these times, one dares not hope to be like this.
Simply conceal your name and obscure your traces, maintaining your proper lot as a weathered old monk of the bone-and-iron mold.

With what you have personally realized and attained, make use of it according to your own capacity to exhaust past karma and harmonize with former habits. If there is surplus energy, extend it to others;
cultivate the conditions for *prajñā* and refine yourself until your footing is pure and mature, like a field left fallow.

If one can sift through the weeds to find even one or two who truly understand, they shall together transcend birth and death and increasingly benefit the future, thereby repaying the profound kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Only when driven by necessity—like frost and dew ripening the fruit—will one emerge into the world to respond to conditions and accord with them, opening the way for humans and devas.
Yet, one must never set the mind upon seeking worldly gain; how much less should one rely on noble power to create a mere semblance of a stream [of disciples]?
The conduct of worldly "masters" deceives the common folk and ignores the sages; seeking profit and fame, they commit deeds of the Avīci Hell.

Even if they lack the karmic conditions for enlightenment, they merely pass their lives in this manner, yet they incur no karmic retribution—they are truly *arhats* who have transcended the net of dust.
A monk asked Emperor Tiantai, "What are precept, concentration, and wisdom? The Emperor replied, "In my place, there is no such idle furniture.
Another asked Deshan, "What is the Buddha? Deshan said, "The Buddha is an old bhikṣu from Western Heaven.
Another asked Shitou, "What is the Way? He answered, "Wood. "What is Chan? He said, "A paving brick. A monk asked Yunmen:
"What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? He replied, "A steamed bun.
Again he asked, "Zhaozhou, what is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? He replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. Again he asked, "Qingping, what is outflow?"
He replied, "A rice-strainer. Again he asked, "The outflow-free (anāsrava). He replied, "A wooden ladle. He asked, "How are the three corners the Three Jewels? He replied, "Rice, millet, and beans.
These are all words of fundamental compassion from the feet of the original masters of former lives, who trod upon solid ground.
If one follows their words, one fails them; yet if one does not follow their words, how else can it be?
To comprehend this—unless one possesses the adamantine eye of right vision, one will not know its point of descent.
This gate of sudden liberation and realization has, until now, never been experienced by anyone. Those who are muddled and blind through clinging to the literal fail to understand it at all;
yet, if one with a sharp-rooted disposition and the spirit of an "Old Man Meng" suddenly penetrates it directly and takes it up, then whenever they require it, they may employ it.

When it comes time to practice, one simply practices. Without such a degree of mental cultivation reaching full maturity, one might suddenly set the mind down in its place and find rest, remaining peaceful and content throughout the day with deep, steady breathing;
this is not necessarily unauthentic. What is most difficult to manage is that which is "halfway forward and halfway back":
having recognized the viewing of light and shadows and hearing sounds, yet failing to follow after them, one must instead guard the nature of profound stillness. Once this is achieved...
Taking this as a supreme treasure held within one’s breast, one remains bright and clear all day long, with a jumble of various knowledges and understandings.
One carries the burden of thinking, "I too have a place of realization; I have once received the seal of approval from a master.

Yet this only serves to increase one's own views, leading one to pass judgment on the ancients and the present, to seal oneself as a successor to the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and to disparage everything else. When questioned, one immediately resorts to clever maneuvers, piling them all together into a single mass of attachment.
Little do they realize that at the very end, they have already mistakenly identified the "pan-star" (the pivot).
When one finally provides them with skillful means to untangle their adhesions and loosen their bonds, they instead claim that the teacher is shifting their perspective or twisting their minds.
To act with such mental conduct—what possible remedy can there be? Only when they suddenly awaken on their own to recognize their error, and subsequently let go of it, will it truly be beneficial.

When knowledge encounters these [obstacles], one must possess great skill and strength to refine them; if one can rescue even a single person or half a person to the point of ultimate penetration, there is no harm in turning the heterodox into the orthodox.
This is truly a person of immeasurable capacity. Why? It is simply because when one has many illnesses, one becomes well-versed in the nature of medicines.

One who has attained the ground has the mental machinations extinguished and the illuminating essence forgotten; there is no longer any discernment, and one simply abides in a state of leisurely ease.
Thus, the devas have no way to offer flowers, and demons or outsiders cannot see even as they lurk in the shadows.

Walking at the bottom of the deep sea, with outflows exhausted and the mind liberated, one’s actions are ordinary, no different from those in a village of three households. One directly lets go of the heart and nurtures this state until—
Even at such a point, he is not willing to remain; as soon as there is the slightest trace [of attachment], he perceives it as being like Mount Tai obstructing him, and he immediately shakes it off.
Although this is purely the ground of principle, even that is not to be grasped. If one grasps at it, it becomes a thorn of views.
Therefore, it is said: "The Way mindlessly merges with the person; the person mindlessly merges with the Way. How could he ever be willing to parade about, saying, "I am"?

One who has attained the fundamental ground originally does not wish for others to know it. This is called "the cessation of study and non-action"; such a person is a peer of the ancients and a true man of the Way.
One day at late noon during a meal, when the old master was descending from his quarters with his alms bowl, Xuefeng said, "The bell has not yet rung."
The drum had not yet sounded; where would Deshan go for alms? Shan bowed his head and turned back.
Hearing this, Yantou said, "Great as he may be, Deshan has still not realized the final word. Deshan asked, "Do you not approve of me, old monk?
Yantou then secretly conveyed his meaning to him. The following day, when Deshan ascended the seat, it was utterly different from his usual manner. Yantou clapped his hands in approval.
He said to the assembly, "I am glad that this old fellow understands the final phrase. Nevertheless, he shall have but three years.
Regarding this kōan, there are many in the monastic communities who offer interpretations; yet few truly penetrate it with certainty. Some say that such a phrase truly exists;
some say that although father and son sang in harmony, such a phrase actually does not exist; and some say that this—
The phrases must be transmitted in secret; otherwise, one will merely increase intellectual understanding and clever maneuvers, which are far removed from the fundamental essence.
Thus it is said: "The supreme flavor of clarified butter is prized by the world, yet when encountered by such people, it turns instead into poison."
He studies the living word (*huoju*), not the dead word (*siju*). If one can realize it under the living word, one will never forget it for eons;
if one realizes it under the dead word, one cannot even save oneself. If you wish to act as a teacher to the patriarchs and Buddhas, you must clearly grasp the living word.
Shaoyang uttered a phrase like a sharp blade that cuts everything away. Linji also said: "The 'blow-off-the-head' sword has been used; it must be quickly polished. This is it.
How could this be a matter of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*)? Nor is it something within the reach of worldly wisdom or clever eloquence.

It is simply to penetrate deeply to the very source, to strike down all former reliance on external interpretations—whether clear or obscure, favorable or adverse—and to seal them with the Diamond Seal of Rightness.
One brandishes the precious sword of the Vajra King and employs one’s own fundamental means. Thus it is said: "To kill a person, one must have the sword that kills; to..."
A person must be a living sword. Having already killed a person, one must be able to bring that person back to life; having already brought them back to life, one must be able to kill them again.
If one remains solitary and isolated, one falls into partiality. At the moment of extending the hand, observe the skillful means (*upāya*);

do not allow the blade to be wounded or the hand to be injured. At every step, there must be a path for emergence. Radiant and unobstructed on all eight sides, it illuminates all other directions. And...
The lower blade must also be held firmly; if it is even slightly loose, one will fall seven or eight times.

Even for something as trivial as oneself, not even a hair’s breadth is spared—if it exists at all, it is cut into three pieces. How much more so for those who are the "fangs and claws" of this Gate from of old?
When encountering such a person, as soon as [the teaching] is brought forth, if it meets the occasion, it is used together with them; if it does not meet the occasion, [it is discarded].
Then one must eradicate them; take this as the essential. There is no matter that will not be understood. It depends entirely on diligent practice.
The Head Seat Huazang Ming has followed me from Jingzhou, Jiaoshan, and Zhongfu for over ten years.

His emotions, attachments, and intellectual understandings have all been stripped away. Having entered this gate, there is no path of illumination, function, or intellectual cleverness that he has not dismantled.

[The Master] set aside [other matters]. Only after being refined a hundred times and tempered a thousand times within the room did he emerge. Zuominlao considered this to be a departure from the norm;
morning and evening, he desired to obtain the Master’s written words. Therefore, I have compiled several chapters and handed them over to him.
To Zhang Xuanfu, Duke and Minister:
In the past, your acquaintance with this Way was exceedingly deep and long-standing; how could it be communicated through mere words and phrases?

Nevertheless, transcending the boundaries of the school and surpassing its traditions is the domain of the great masters of vast vision. Though their mastery may manifest in a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, it never departs from the grasp of their own hands.

The worldly dharmas and the Buddha-dharmas have never been different. Only when one uses daily life to illuminate and realize that the mind is like a mirror—wherein images and traces are from the outset never lost to its reflection—is this the Great Samādhi.

Therefore, Vimalakīrti took food from the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) realm, borrowed a seat from the King of Lamps (Dīparāja), compressed the World of Wondrous Joy (Abhirati) like a potter’s wheel, contained Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed, and drew the fires of the kalpa into his own belly. By means of these [powers],...
The palms turn over. Within, the center is empty yet spiritual, tranquil yet illuminating; externally, phenomena emerge and subside, revolving without relying on external force.
This is what is called realizing the inconceivable—all occurs within the square inch of one’s own field of consciousness.

How much more so for those who build merit and establish achievements, who harbor virtue and practice sincerity, finding the source at every turn. Grasping the diamond sword, they wield the power of killing and giving life.

At the moment the staff-bearer gives his command, all is this very marvel. To hope for words to express what lies beyond the external—though it be ten thousand miles away—it is as if one were witnessing it with one's own eyes.
Furthermore:
Since antiquity, sages and worthies of extraordinary capacity and superior talent have uniquely realized this great causal nexus by planting the roots of a great vessel.
Through the power of their compassionate vows, they have manifested and directly pointed to this matter—most profound and most abstruse—which is the single essence of all phenomena.
Without establishing any rungs on a ladder, they transcend suddenly and attain it alone; from before the empty kalpa, they have been serene and unmoving, sealing and certifying all spirits.
The fundamental ground: it spans past and present, transcending thought and deliberation; it goes beyond the holy and the mundane, surpassing knowledge and views.
From the very beginning, it is unshakable—purely naked and vibrantly alive. Among all sentient and insentient beings in the present, there is none that does not fully possess it.

Therefore, at his first birth, Śākyamuni immediately pointed to heaven and earth and let out a great roar, bringing it forth directly before him. Next, he used the morning star; finally, he brought it up once more.
Flowers. It is only precious when one possesses this eye of correct vision and realizes it for oneself. Since then, the [lineages of] the Four Sevens and Two Threes have been transmitted in secret.

Those who do not know this think there are some subtle functions or divine mechanisms at play; they merely say one follows the waves and drifts with the current, never investigating the fundamental root.
If one were to exhaustively investigate the ultimate meaning, it would not require even a single note. Formerly, when Prince Li saw Shimen, Shimen said:

He said, "This is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. Li immediately took charge and presented his own statement in verse: "To study the Way, one must be an iron man.
When the hand touches the heart, one must be prepared to give it all. Directly heading for supreme Bodhi, One need not concern oneself with any right or wrong.
This was because his superior wisdom, keen faculties, and celestial potential were already complete; he sought only to achieve genuine and thorough penetration.
When utilizing it, one grasps the great pivot to unleash the great function; acting prior to the stimulus, it turns apart from all things.
Yantou said: "To turn back objects is superior; to pursue objects is inferior. If we speak of battle, everyone’s strength lies in the point of turning.
If one can turn swiftly upon objects, then all will stand downwind and come under one's own grasp, captured.

Whether unrolling or rolling up [the teachings], all may be transformed and realized. In daily life, one dwells in a state of natural composure and tranquility, with not even a thread of attachment clinging to the mind.
Moving in response to circumstances, one naturally wields the celestial pivot; through transformation and penetration, one attains great mastery.
The myriad phenomena and myriad conditions are all resolved as easily as a blade cutting through bamboo, falling like grass before the wind. Thus, it is established.
Since its abiding place is real, it possesses power when in operation; how much more so when leading heroes and driving troops as fierce as leopards and tigers!
To repel great invaders, comfort the myriad people, stabilize the state, and assist in the enterprise of restoration—all depends solely on this one move to pivot the essential hinge above.
This is a merit that shall not be uprooted for ten thousand generations, shared by you and the ancient Buddhas in seeing, hearing, knowing, and realizing.
Regarding this application: The Fourth Patriarch said, "If it is not the mind, do not ask about the Buddha. Deshan said, "The Buddha is simply a person of no affairs.
Yongjia said, "Without departing from this very place, it is ever serene; seek it and you will know that it cannot be seen.
The "Person of No Rank" constantly enters and exits through the gate of the face. All these are but manifestations of this very same essence.
Now, the Grand Chancellor of the Bureau of Military Affairs has already grasped this beyond words and transcended it before sounds;

yet, I, a mere rustic with idle talk, have been remiss in my shortcomings. Having been humbly favored by your sagacious compassion and thus enlightened, I have cast aside the wisdom of an old farmer, an old gardener, or an old horse, and present this humble offering of wild herbs.

Master Yuan, the Head Seat, is a man who has attained the Way; his standing place is solitary, perilous, and steeply precipitous. He does not set himself in opposition to a single dharma, and when he acts, not even a speck of dust is stirred.
This goes far beyond merely entering a forest without moving the grass or entering water without disturbing the waves; it is because his inner being is already empty and still.

Externally severing the effort of illumination, one attains spontaneity; penetratingly realizing the state of no-mind, even if ten thousand affairs suddenly descend upon one, how could they disturb the spirit or interfere with one’s deliberations?
In ordinary times, one simply maintains the state of leisurely stillness, appearing as if dull-witted or dazed. Yet when facing phenomena, one does not employ any artifice;
when it comes to resolving matters, like a whirlwind or a flash of lightning, there is nothing that does not accord with the occasion. How could this be...?

This is not something maintained by mere habit. Therefore, the ancient masters said: "It is like a person learning archery; only after a long time does one hit the mark. Yet, once awakened, it occurs in a single instant.
The cultivation of practice must rely on a long duration. It is like a young pigeon that, upon being born, is bare-boned and naked;
as it is nurtured and fed over a long period of time, its feathers and plumage eventually form, and it is then able to fly high and far."
The point is this: to awaken to and thoroughly penetrate the essential principle of subduing [the mind].
For instance, although the various sensory realms constantly flow within, for one who has reached the ultimate state, there is nothing that is not empty and unobstructed;

it is entirely one’s own great gate of liberation. Though acting all day long, one never truly acts; there is no longing or aversion, nor is there any weariness. Having thus exhausted [all delusions], one...

Since all things are devoid of subject and object, how much less could there be the arising of weariness or regression? If one’s nature is by disposition partial or deficient, one should especially augment those capacities one lacks.

By liberating oneself through the perfect penetration of the teachings, one should sing in harmony with the Dharma to gather and transform others; by opening up the provisional means, one responds to all situations with grace and composure, ensuring that whether high or low, far or near, there is not the slightest error.
One should constantly practice the conduct of Never-Disparaging and emulate the Immortal of Forbearance, following the tracks of the Buddhas of the past.

[He] accomplishes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), makes firm the practice of the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*), and reaches the stage where great function manifests before one, such that clamor and stillness are of one essence.
Like a boat descending a river, it requires no labor of oar or pole; he blends and encompasses all, perfectly realizing the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
He is thus a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of both the mundane and supramundane realms. As an ancient worthy said: "In even a village of three households, one must..."
Within these monastic communities, even in places where no such community exists, those of noble aspiration likewise prefer their own ease.

When things have reached such a state, it is all the more necessary to maintain firm adherence; this depends solely on exerting oneself with tireless diligence. Ultimately, the same applies to the bustling and the quiet:

while moving through and responding to changes within the bustle, one remains inwardly empty and still; and in the quiet, one is not bound by that stillness. Thus, one follows along as circumstances dictate.
Wherever one goes, all things are the means of one's livelihood; however, only those who possess a fundamental basis—being inwardly empty and outwardly compliant—can achieve this.
Generally speaking, one who acts as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) should be compassionate, gentle, and harmonious in receiving others, dwelling in equanimity and non-contention.
Even when others approach with malice, or when they inflict upon me harsh words, ill repute, or offensive forms and sounds, or when they unjustly interfere and slander me...

Regarding insults and humiliation, simply withdraw and reflect within yourself; ensure you have no cause for regret. Do not engage in any comparison with them, nor stir thoughts of anger or resentment.
Simply cut it off directly, as if from the very beginning you had neither heard nor seen it. After a long time, demonic afflictions will naturally vanish.
If you engage in comparison with them, malicious words will only rebound upon you—how could there ever be an end to this? Furthermore, it does not manifest your own [virtue].
How does your own strength differ from that of the common stream? Exert yourself to practice it with all your might; naturally, there will be none who do not submit.

Under the stroke of the mallet and the flick of the whisk, you shall awaken those in the realms of humans and devas, enabling them to break through and escape birth and death—how could this be a minor cause and condition?

You should maintain a tranquil and harmonious expression and demeanor to guide and lead others according to their capacity, examining them in response to their questions. Discern the origins of their practice, verify their state of being, and strike at their particular biases.

It causes one to fall. It seizes away that which one clings to, directly pointing it out so that one may see the Buddha-nature and reach the field of great rest and great peace—what is called "pulling out the nails and extracting the wedges," "loosening the glue and removing the bonds.
One must by no means use real dharmas to entangle people, causing them to dwell thus or grasp thus; do not allow others to shift or overturn you. This is a poison. It causes...
He has consumed his entire life carrying a wooden board; how could such deception possibly bring any benefit?

The Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared in the world specifically to proclaim this great causal connection, which is called the "Single Transmission of the Mind-Seal" (chuanxin yin) where no words or letters are established.
It addresses those of the highest capacity through speech and phrases, valuing nothing more than awakening upon hearing it once; one must directly take responsibility for it and then practice.
Seeking neither fame nor gain, he devoted himself solely to penetrating through and liberation from birth and death. Now that you have become his descendant, you must preserve his legacy.
Observe how, in ancient times, there were many men of the Way who, upon their every movement, subdued dragons and tamed tigers;

they received the precepts from the divine spirits, endured bitter hardships and ate plain food, utterly forgetting the human world and forever bidding farewell to the mundane realm. For twenty or thirty years, they [endured] broken-legged...

Cooking rice in a cauldron to eat, they conceal their traces and obscure their names, often passing away while sitting or standing. Among them, one or two were pushed forward by the various sages to establish the ancestral style;
there were none who did not maintain lofty conduct and strive to repay the Buddha’s kindness by circulating the Great Dharma.
From the very first word or half-sentence they uttered, it was done out of sheer necessity; though they knew full well that these were merely expedients for guiding people into the Way.
The gate of principle is the very tile that knocks upon it; its structure, power, and function may well serve as a model for future generations.
You should take this as your standard and exhort one another to strive toward restoring the ancient style. Most of all, avoid seeking fame or pursuing trivial gain—this is my earnest wish.

In the past, when Mazu returned to his hometown, he was criticized for using a winnowing basket; fearing that this would hinder his practice of the Way, he subsequently crossed the Gorges and established connections in Jiangxi.
In the past, when Daosui returned to his hometown, he first spent three years at the mouth of Longhuai providing tea and soup to cultivate karmic conditions with the assembly.

The Record of Conduct by Benji also need not be restricted by whether things are discarded or retained.

The three great masters—Huanglong, Cuiyan, and the others—had their descendants spread throughout the world; indeed, they did not fail the trust entrusted to them.

Under the gate of the Patriarchs, there were those who severed their arms, stood in the snow, used their waists as millstones, pounded grain with mortars and pestles, carried wheat, pushed carts, worked in gardens, prepared meals, reclaimed fields, served hot water and tea, hauled earth, and pulled millstones.

Only those who resist worldly desires, transcend the mundane, exert themselves without ceasing, and strive to achieve success are capable of such deeds. What is this? It is the realization of the Way.

To Shi Yu, the Secretary (Buddhist Monk). (Chan Master Fozhi, residing at Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou):

Not even a hair’s breadth [of movement]. Deeply still and凝然 (unmoving), it is something that Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot know, and which demons and outsiders cannot grasp.

In this way, they can extensively deliver others through the Great Dharma, continue the ancestral lamp, and be worthy of repaying the unrepayable debt of gratitude.
In the past, when the old Chan Master Nan of Huanglong had not yet seen Shishuang, he possessed a whole belly full of Chan.

One must strive to reach the ultimate limit and exhaust all possibilities; do not remain like one who guards a stump waiting for a hare, nor mistake a finger for the moon.
Discernment must lie before the movement of the occasion; even the stirring of dust or a blade of grass is illuminated by its very inception, let alone the constant clamor of social interaction.
If the breast is not empty and still, with not a single dharma obstructing the mind, how could one respond perfectly without error, anticipating the occasion to illuminate all things?
All of these are the effects of the *nāga* remaining in meditative concentration:

Having passed through these stages over a long period, the Master of the Great Liberation—who possesses the correct eye—transformed conventional patterns and opened up the common path, ensuring that his followers do not stagnate in names and forms nor fall into mere abstract principle.

It is entirely this very moment. Only those who have stepped upon the pivotal lock of the ultimate direction can truly understand it.

Only when every trace of biased attachment and doubt had been completely shattered could they be led to let go entirely, attain a steady footing, and transform until reaching a ground that cannot be broken.
It is like a mold for casting a vessel: one must first ensure it is properly sealed before releasing the contents to serve others and benefit living beings. This is no small matter;

if there is even a single imperfection, the mold itself will be distorted. Once cast, the resulting object will be uneven with seven hollows and eight protrusions, becoming a laughingstock to its maker.

His conduct was as pure as ice or jade; outwardly, he was versatile and harmonious, observing the sentiments of the multitude and skillfully adapting to them.

Tilling the soil and seizing [the harvest] while the spirits of hunger remain unfathomable—relying solely upon the single Great Liberation, one no longer arises within the marks of disparate species.
With horns and head perfectly settled in non-action, this is truly the Arhat who transcends the dust through the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Deeds.
As Bodhidharma said: "When practice and understanding correspond, one is called a Patriarch."

This serves to clarify the causal conditions of the Great Matter. This principle of mutual necessity and mutual support has been so since antiquity.

To have answers that accord with whatever questions are asked, yet remain profoundly still and silent even when unasked—is this not the essential thread for truly penetrating through and beyond birth and death?

The final phrase penetrates everything: whether there is speech or silence, upward or downward, provisional or ultimate, illumination or function, unfolding or rolling up, bestowing or taking away—it all does not require anything other than being thoroughly scrutinized and understood. Who can recognize this "knob" (babi) of Zhaozhou?
One must be of our own spiritual lineage to do so.
The former Vice-Abbot Ning showed that for such a great cause and condition, whenever masters and disciples met, they never failed to strike and uplift one another with this.
From eating and sleeping to moments of leisure and seclusion, there was nothing in which they did not apply their mindfulness to this. Therefore, every word and every phrase is indeed a staff.

Then he gave a shout; every movement of his eyes and gestures was capable of striking the vital point. This was because his sincere mind was single-minded and free from the pollution of many evil thoughts and views;
thus, directly accepting [the truth] seemed not difficult. Nowadays, however, the faculties of my fellow practitioners are dull and further corrupted by confusion.
Although they have sought out spiritual teachers and been steeped in their teachings for a long time, they still harbor hesitation and cannot proceed with single-minded resolve.

Thorough realization depends on whether one’s practice is consistent and sustained over a long period. If you can devote yourself to the Way without ceasing day or night, forgetting sleep and food in your diligent efforts, you need not fear falling short of the ancients.

It is shown that for a practitioner of Chan who has resolved their will to cultivate the Way, throughout the twelve hours of day and night, they must self-reflect and self-realize, keeping this in mind at all times.
They should know that beneath their own feet lies a great causal connection—one that does not increase when dwelling among the holy nor decrease when abiding among the ordinary. It is unique...

Having liberated itself from the roots and objects of the senses, it transcends far beyond the realm of phenomena. Whatever it performs does not establish fixed positions; it is quiescent, profound, and immovable.

Amidst ten thousand transformations and a thousand changes, it remains fundamentally unshaken. Manifesting in response to conditions, it unfolds upon encountering circumstances, achieving perfect completion in all things.
One must simply be empty and still, so that all things transcend. When the fundamental source is clarified, there is no depth of mystery it does not illuminate.

Ten thousand years are a single thought-moment; a single thought-moment is ten thousand years. Penetrating to the very top and bottom, this is the total function of the Great Activity. It is like a strong man extending or contracting his arm—in an instant, without borrowing any external power.
Thus, the illusory cataracts of birth and death are forever extinguished, and the adamantine true body is uniquely revealed. Once attained, it is eternal.

There shall be no interruption. The teachings of the ancients and the present, the karmic conditions, the public cases (*gong'an*), the questions and answers, and the functional applications are all complete.
If you clarify this and practice it with such vigor that the days and years deepen, you will naturally encounter the source at every turn and everything will be forged into a single whole.
Have you not seen what Faden said: "Entering a desolate field, one does not discriminate; taking up whatever grass comes to hand, it meets the eye."
It has never existed. Why do you not speak when the opportunity arises? Rootless yet it lives; detached from the ground yet it does not fall.
If you do not even recognize its use in daily life, where else will you seek it? You must carefully investigate this.

To the Zen practitioner Shih-hui, it is told that when Shui-lao visited Mazu and asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, Mazu gave him a kick. Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment and said:
"The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings are all found by recognizing the source upon a single hair-tip."
"How joyful! he exclaimed, laughing heartily. He continued until his lifelong maxim for the assembly was established:
"Ever since I took one bite from Master Ma’s kick, I have laughed without ceasing until this very day. Again, he laughed heartily.

This was because, despite his sincere and resolute efforts to find a point of entry, he had not yet attained it; suddenly encountering the kick, he accepted it in its entirety and took it upon himself.
One must penetrate through to liberation without doubt. Then, one should expel from the breast whatever has been realized and no longer concern oneself with other matters.
If one’s present study is truly authentic, when a master hurls at one a single word, a single phrase, a single pivot, or a single scene, one will turn upon being struck.
How could there be any difficulty? The only worry is that one's faculties are floating and consciousness shallow, drifting like the wind passing over the tops of trees.
Even if one were to uphold and recite this a thousand or ten thousand times, one would still be unable to attain immediate realization;

how much less so for those who, through intellectual interpretation, point to it as being "non-existent," thereby failing to enter into such awakening? Master Ma Shuilao also established his teaching in this very manner for a time.
If this were so, one would not have even dreamed of it until the year of the donkey. Therefore, in studying the Way, one values only sincere faith;
as for those who practice wisdom and meditation, their conduct must be extremely focused. I have briefly set this forth merely to demonstrate a skillful means.
If one discusses this matter, it is like the spark struck from flint or a flash of lightning. Whether you understand it clearly or not, you cannot avoid losing your body and life.
Now, while it is certainly true that failing to understand clearly leads to the loss of body and life, why is it that even understanding it clearly results in the loss of body and life?
Many people reach this point and become stuck in doubt; yet they fail to realize that only upon reaching the ultimate end does one truly arrive.
At the point where the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is severed, one exchanges out one’s heart, liver, and five viscera to become equal with that which is above.
Therefore it is said: "Directly beneath, it is like letting go from a precipice. Only then is one forged from cast iron;
this is called "penetrating through the thicket of thorns" and not doubting the tongues of the old masters of the world. One may then truly possess the capacity for authentic study.
To those who cultivate the Way, such as Venerable Xuruan:
A student of the Way who has first developed faith and aspiration may grow weary of the world’s turmoil and anxieties, constantly fearing they will be unable to find a way of entry.

Having encountered the teacher’s pointing-out instruction, some may suddenly realize it for themselves directly beneath them: that from the very beginning, they have possessed the wondrously perfect true mind in its entirety.

Upon encountering objects and conditions, they recognize their own falling into attachment; they then cling to this state, suffering from an inability to emerge from it, and thus create a conceptual nest.
Within the sphere of sensory stimuli, they establish illumination and function, uttering shouts, striking with their hands, rolling their eyes, and brandishing their eyebrows.
This single instance of raising the eyebrows was quite extraordinary. Yet, when one encounters a true master of the school, all such intellectual understandings are stripped away.
One then directly realizes the original state that is unconditioned, effortless, and mindless.
Only after this does one recognize shame and know how to rest, becoming entirely silent and still; even the Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot find its point of origin, let alone others. Therefore:

Yantou said: "He who has attained merely maintains a state of idle ease; throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, he is without desire and without dependence—is this not the Dharma-gate of peace and happiness?"
In the past, Guankui went to Moshan. Moshan asked, "Where have you recently departed from? Guankui replied, "From the crossroads.
Moshan said, "Why did you not cover it over? Guankui was speechless. On the following day, he posed another question: "What is the realm of Moshan? Moshan replied, "The crown is not revealed."
"What is it like to be a person among the mountains? He replied, "It is neither male nor female, nor any such form. Xixian asked, "How can you not change?
Deshan said, "I am neither a spirit nor a ghost; what would there be to change? Is this not treading firmly on the ground and arriving at the place where the cliffs stand ten thousand fathoms high?
Therefore it is said: "The final word is where one first reaches the secure barrier; it cuts off the vital ford."
It makes no distinction between ordinary beings and sages. Since it was so for the ancients, how could it be lacking for people today? Fortunately, there is the precious sword of the Vajra King;
when one encounters a true知音 (a person of like mind), it must be brought forth.
To the Chan practitioner Liang Lu-tou:
The golden-colored dhūta sat in meditation for kalpas at Mount Kukkutapāda; Bodhidharma faced the wall for nine years at Shaolin;
Caoxi stayed in Sishui County watching hunters; Dayi established a hermitage in the deep mountains for ten years; and Damei remained in one place, cutting off all human contact.
As for the traces: Wuye read through the Great Canon; the ancient sage stood on one foot for seven days and nights to praise Tiṣya;
Sadāprarudita spent a month selling his heart and liver; Changqing sat until he wore through seven cushions—all of these were for the sake of this single great causal connection.

Such an aspiration is worthy of admiration; it shall serve as a standard for future generations forever. Even if one must remain upon a long bed in the infirmary, it is no more than an occasion to settle the mind and investigate reality.
One need only ensure that the mental state is clear and still; it is precisely amidst the clamor and turmoil that one should apply diligent effort.
When applying this effort, one must penetrate to the very top and bottom without the slightest omission, so that the whole body is fully manifested.
This realization does not arise from oneself or another; it is simply this one great capacity turning and rolling like a wheel.
To further explain the ultimate truth of the Buddha-dharma, maintain it with a level and steady hand. As days pass and years deepen, it will naturally become firm and solid beneath the feet.
This is nothing other than the Venerable Liang directly realizing and verifying it—like water entering water, like gold being traded for gold. It is even.
To be equal and one, serene, true, and pure—this is the living practice of liberation. Simply let not a single thought arise, and allow it to be luminously clear.
As soon as there is right and wrong, self and other, gain and loss, do not follow after them; this is to personally attend upon one’s own true spiritual friend day and night.
Why worry that this matter will not be accomplished? You must examine yourself with urgency.
Shi Xu Fengyi (Tinggui): This matter is not difficult for those of sharp faculties and superior wisdom who, upon hearing it once, attain a thousandfold awakening.
However, one must have firm and solid roots, possess a thorough and authentic conviction, maintain steadfastness, and be able to act as the master. Amidst all circumstances of adversity or favor...

The causes and conditions of differentiation are forged into a single whole, like the great void, without the slightest obstruction or partition. It is profoundly still and luminously empty, without change or transformation.
Though one undergoes hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, it remains from beginning to end as a single state, once attained, forever stable and secure.

I have often seen those who are clever, brilliant, and quick-witted, yet whose faculties are floating and whose footing is shallow; they immediately recognize change within words and phrases, and thus take the mundane...

Finding no further point at which to pass beyond, they instead cause the thorns of views to grow, indulging in their own abilities and intellectual understandings, and chasing after the sharpness and fluency of speech.
They take this to be the entirety of the Buddha-dharma; yet when it comes to the arising of conditions within actual experience, they fail to penetrate or transcend them.

Consequently, they fall into progress and retreat, which is truly lamentable. Therefore, the ancients truly underwent thousands of demons and myriad hardships, experiencing them all completely. Although [the path] is seven...
Even when subjected to mutilation, he did not stir a thought; his resolve was as firm as iron or stone.
Thus, he attained liberation from birth and death without expending any effort at all. Is this not the very spirit of a great man, transcending emotions and acting with noble magnanimity?
For a lay bodhisattva to cultivate the practices of renunciation is like a lotus growing from fire; for fame, status, power, reality, and ambition are by nature difficult to subdue.
How much more so in the burning house, where one is tormented by a hundred ends and a thousand threads of turmoil?

Unless one directly realizes one's own original, true, wondrous, and perfect nature and reaches the field of rest in great tranquil concentration, it will be especially difficult to let go and attain vast, level equanimity.
Constantly and thoroughly realizing the state of no-mind, one contemplates all phenomena as being like dreams and illusions—an empty and vast expanse.

One should, according to the time and circumstances, dispel and set them aside. Thus, one shares the same fundamental cause as Vimalakīrti, the Great Master Fu, Prime Minister Pei, and Grand Secretary Yang, as well as other eminent lay practitioners.
According to one's own capacity, one transforms those who have not yet awakened, leading them together into the state of non-attainment.
Within the ocean of the dharma-nature of non-action, it is not a waste of one's fundamental essence to come forth once more to this Jambudvīpa and strike out a single blow.
There is not much to the Buddha-dharma: like Jūzhi pointing a finger, or Baizhang striking the ground—just striking the ground; or Niutou blowing on his robe.
Fur. No karma, no deluded thoughts. Zhongyi’s “Da da he he. The ancient embankment has no Buddha-nature. “Gucha” (Bone-crushing)—for a lifetime he spoke only of this “bone-crushing.
It was precisely because he could believe it thoroughly that he enjoyed its benefits for his entire life without exhaustion.
If you harbor doubt, then divergent views and distinctions will arise; there will be an "upward" and a "downward" direction, and how could you ever sit firmly in certainty? Regarding this:
To value long-term endurance is indeed rare among men.
Once you have entered the fundamental ground with clear penetration, you must become liberated, standing out uniquely, solitary and precarious like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms.
The sicknesses of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are cast off; the mysterious and wondrous rationality is discarded. In this state of ordinary vastness, one knows nothing at all.

It will not. Just as people in a village of three households have no difference from the start, if one nurtures them for a long time, through many years and months, they become simple and honest, finding great peace and only then attaining true happiness. In the end, they are unwilling to reveal themselves, acting clever or displaying skillful means;
they do not flaunt their knowledge or pursue mere verbal Zen. Therefore it is said: "Out of ten words, nine hit the mark."
It is just like this. Furthermore, it is said that among thousands or hundreds of people, there are only those seeking to become Buddhas;
yet, among them, it is difficult to find even one person who is a "pathless Way-man" (wuxin daoren). This matter most requires diligent practice.

In such practice, not clinging to appearances and not dwelling upon merit is called "formless true cultivation. It is like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, cutting straight through the current. Thus it is.
In practicing the Way, one should not allow even a drop of water or a speck of ice to remain within the breast, let alone deliberately giving rise to the mind that commits various evils.
Having protected oneself in this manner, one likewise exhorts those who have not yet awakened.
Thus, upon this very point, one becomes upright, purely faithful, and free from striving or affairs—is this not a joy?

This great Dharma, which harmonizes with and brings understanding to all, has been realized by the Buddhas of the three periods of time and transmitted together by the patriarchs of successive generations.

Sealed by a single seal, it points directly to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha; it does not rely on written words or phrases, and is thus called the "separate transmission outside the teachings."

The mind-seal is transmitted directly. If one enters the path of verbal explanation, establishing stages and rungs, and engaging in conceptual deliberation regarding what lies beyond or within the extraordinary, then one loses the fundamental school and fails the ancient sages.
One must, at the very outset of entering practice, encounter a person of the true lineage.

Directly cut off the root and retreat to rely upon yourself. With an iron-like heart, cast away at once and to the bottom all former deluded thoughts, views, worldly wisdom, eloquence, and the notions of self and other, gain and loss. Be, in this very moment, like withered wood or dead ashes.

When emotions are exhausted and views are eliminated, one arrives at a state of pure nakedness and stark clarity. There, one suddenly realizes and attains enlightenment, not differing by even a single hair’s breadth from the sages of antiquity.
When one has attained such profound faith and reached such thorough insight, this is truly the gateway for entering into principle.

Furthermore, one must be taught that "one thought-moment is ten thousand years, and ten thousand years are one thought-moment," maintaining this single-minded focus throughout the two periods of six hours [day and night].
There is no admixture. As soon as even a speck of dust arises or ceases, one falls into the twenty-five realms of existence, with no prospect of escape.

Even unto death, one must vainly struggle to bite through the teachings; only then will the ground be stable and secure, such that one cannot be confined within the ranks of either sage or ordinary being.
This is the beginning of being like a bird escaping its cage, resting of itself and understanding of itself. Having attained this state, one puts on the robes;

like true gold refined a hundred times, every movement and action is carefree and vast. The relationship between the sense faculties and their objects, and the realms of birth-and-death and wisdom, are as profound and subtle as snow melted by boiling water.
Thus, one spontaneously knows the proper time and has nothing further to add; this is called being a "mindless person.
By means of this practice and realization, one further awakens those who have not yet awakened and causes them to tread this path accordingly. Is this not the essential Way?
For the sake of this very matter, the ancients did not merely forget their meals and neglect their sleep;
they went so far as to sacrifice their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains, or to cut off their arms and carry grain for grinding, doing so for as long as twenty or thirty years.

Take, for instance, Yantou, Xuefeng, and Qinshan, who, though they traveled together through the monastic forests, each took up a different task and served with diligence nine times over. Or consider Dongshan, who went to Touzi three times; in all such instances—

Wherever they went, they never let a single night or a single moment pass in vain. They invariably compared their progress with one another and refined each other through mutual critique, thereby attaining a profound realization.
Xinfeng Huo understood the essential meaning, while Deqiao observed his every step and the structure of his practice; they may truly be called dragons and elephants within the Dharma-gate.
Those of later generations can look up to their established tracks and must not allow their time to be wasted in vain, thereby bringing shame upon those who came before.

Excellent! In the past, National Teacher Tiantai Shao, possessing outstanding talent from his youth, traveled through the monastic forests (*saṃghārāma*). Wherever he went, he immediately grasped the essential pivot and was entrusted with the master’s seat.
Finally, he arrived at the assembly of the Great Dharma-Eye Chan Master Qingliang in Jinling; having grown weary of formal inquiry and consultation, he remained there—only...

He urged those who attended him to follow him as he tucked up his robes and entered the meditation hall. One day, while following the assembly for a formal visit, someone asked, "What is the single drop of water from Cao’s spring?
He replied, "It is the single drop of water from Cao’s spring. Upon hearing this, the Master’s previous intellectual understanding dissolved like melting ice;
only then did he attain great peace and stability. Thus we know that the learning and understanding derived from others account for only one-tenth of what is truly realized.
To speak of a single phrase, a single faculty, or a single object merely increases one's erudition.
To reach the ultimate and the place of true reality, one must have the bottom of the bucket fall out; this matter is definitively not contained within words and phrases.
If one clings to memorization as one’s own realization, it is like a painted cake—how could it ever satisfy hunger? Yet those of great attainment transcend and realize the truth itself.
When it comes to seizing the opportune moment, one transcends conventional tracks within the space of words and phrases. The realm of the pivot and the trap-net cannot ensnare him;
he remains unconfined by them. For instance, when Shitou asked Yueshan, "What are you doing here? he replied, "I do nothing."
Touzi said, "If that is so, then one sits idly. Touzi replied, "Sitting idly is precisely what is done. Touzi asked again, "In your way, you do not 'do'—what is it that you do not do?
Touzi replied, "Even the thousand sages do not know it. Touzi then praised him with this verse:
"From the beginning we have lived together, yet its name is unknown; Spontaneously following along, we simply walk thus. Since antiquity, even the most eminent sages..."
They still do not understand it. How could ordinary people in their haste ever clarify it? Is such a person not one who has attained thorough realization?

How could the mechanisms of speech, his capacity for expression, or his words and phrases ever constrain him? If he were not clear regarding the ground of principle, there would be something obstructing his mind.
The question is like dragging a cat across a felt rug. Therefore, the Patriarch said: "The mind turns following the myriad objects;
where it turns, it is truly profound. If you recognize your nature while following the flow, there will be neither joy nor sorrow."
The initial inquiry of the brothers of the monastic groves possesses the primary cause [of enlightenment].

Before a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), they personally declare that the matter of birth and death is great and their own affairs remain unclarified. Inferring from these words, how could this be merely for the sake of fame, rank, self-importance, or seeking superiority?
If one maintains this mind consistently from beginning to end, one will not worry that one’s own affairs remain unclarified, nor will one...

Having associated with him for some time, yet finding not even a hair’s breadth of resonance within one's own being, one begins to deliberate on what he is like or is not—measuring the length or brevity of his views and thereby increasing one's own self-view.
Seeking a way out, one thinks, "In the future, I shall not dare to fail this single incense offering to the Master.
Little do they realize that they have lost the original primary cause and have instead fallen into...
The realm of Māra departs. An ancient said: "Even if one possesses a retinue and adornments, they will not come; one must arrive at them oneself.
Since we are all equally those who have already trampled through our straw sandals, we ought to fulfill our original aspiration. To resolve to transcend birth and death is of the utmost importance.
Time does not wait for anyone; each of you should exert yourselves.
To show the path for those on the way of Chan meditation: awakening and realization must first be preceded by the establishment of one's resolve.

To desire, from the very outset as a bound ordinary person at the stage of the "vast ground," to stride forward and directly realize the state of a sage and enter the realm of the holy—how could this not require more than minor causes and conditions? One must certainly wield a heart of iron and stone to cut off the flow of birth and death.
One should take up and realize the original, true nature (*dharmatā*). Seeing not even a speck of dust, one perceives no phenomena existing within or without.

Thus, the mind becomes clear and bright, entirely free from obstruction. All actions and functions emerge from this fundamental source. Once the foundation is firm and solid, one can transform all things;
this is called the "Vajra True Body," once attained, attained forever. How could it ever require seeking from without? Therefore, the Ancients said:

Dechun, it is difficult to attain the subtle essence of this school. You must apply yourself with meticulous care; therein, you may suddenly awaken to the true cause, which is the very stepping-stone for transcending the mundane world.
The ancient masters called out across the river while holding up a fan; as soon as they blew upon the dog’s fur, there was a point where the karmic trigger was set off.

Even when [the master] struck the mouth with a spittoon or split the back with a staff, one could understand that the bottom of the bucket had fallen away. This is because through long-term single-minded devotion, in a single moment of sudden awakening, how could this be something obtained from without?
It is entirely due to self-realization and self-awakening.
Dàmé consulted Master Mǎ about receiving the teaching "this very mind is Buddha," whereupon he entered deeply into its innermost essence and went away to dwell in the mountains.
Later, upon hearing the words "neither mind nor Buddha," he remarked: "This old fellow is merely playing with people's sons and daughters;
when will it ever end? You may say 'neither mind nor Buddha,' but I simply maintain 'this very mind is Buddha. Is this not [the case]?
To gaze against the current of the waves is to see through Mazu’s slip.
Yaoshan addressed the assembly, saying: "I have a phrase; I will tell it to you once the calf gives birth to a child.
Had he not let this pass at that time, he would simply have said to him: "Even sitting, you have failed."
To the attendant Shixin:
The essential point of studying the Way lies in deepening one's roots and strengthening the foundation. During the twelve periods of day and night, you must illuminate your own fundamental nature.
You should give rise to a great resolve; when nothing else disturbs the mind, there is a seamless, boundless integration—a state of total emptiness and stillness. All things...
It is because there has never been any doubt; this is called the manifestation of one's own fundamental reality.
Yet, as soon as even a hair’s breadth of intellectual understanding arises, and one wishes to take hold of it as a sovereign master, one immediately falls into the realm of the five aggregates.

One becomes ensnared by seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and by gain and loss, right and wrong. Half-drunk and half-awake, one is unable to settle the mind. To speak of the ultimate truth: it is simply amidst the clamor.
Within the midst of clamor, one manages and carries out [action]; yet it is not like even a single thing. Penetrating to the very top and bottom, it is directly and completely perfected.

Being utterly devoid of form or characteristics, it does not expend effort or utility, yet it does not hinder activity. Whether speaking or remaining silent, whether arising or falling, it is ultimately no other than oneself.
Should even a hair’s breadth of obstruction be perceived, it is entirely delusive thought. One must simply make it flow freely and unimpeded, like the great void.
Emptiness is like a bright mirror upon its stand, like the radiant sun adorning the sky. Whether moving or still, whether coming or going, it is not obtained from without.
Let it be free and at ease; do not be bound by phenomena, nor seek liberation through phenomena. From beginning to end, everything is forged into a single whole.
Where could there be worldly phenomena apart from the Buddha-dharma? Where could there be anything else apart from worldly phenomena?
The Buddha-Dharma exists. For this reason, the Patriarchs point directly to the human mind. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* values people’s detachment from signs.
It is like a strong man extending or contracting his arm in an instant, without relying on external force. Such a realization is essential;
you must long practice retreating inward to investigate, so as to attain a place of definitive, true realization where every thought-moment is pervasive. This is it.
One must encounter boundless and immeasurable great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). To believe with earnest sincerity and strive diligently in one's practice is the most excellent of excellences.
This was shown to the novice monk Zuyin.
Yongjia said: "The Way does not depart from its proper place; it is ever serene. If you seek it, you will know that it cannot be seen.
This means that by remaining serene in the very place where you are, you cut off both extremes and achieve stability. You must absolutely avoid seeking through intellectual understanding;
as soon as you seek, it is like trying to catch a shadow.
Mazu said, "The very mind is Buddha. He also said, "Neither mind nor Buddha. He further said, "Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.
Dongsi said, "Mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. The sword has long since departed, yet you are only now marking the boat.
If one follows each of these words, how could there be a definitive doctrine? If one forgets the words to realize the truth through direct experience, then even if one were to proclaim it again...
To expound hundreds of billions of phrases does not transcend a single reality. Now, what is this place of reality? As Damei said:
"You simply say 'neither mind nor Buddha'; I say 'this very mind is Buddha. Is this not reality? You must have thorough conviction;
you must personally realize and personally see it, so that you naturally cannot be deceived by others."

Shi Minzhi, a descendant in the Dharma lineage of Master Zhao of Daci Temple in Jin’guan who had inherited his transmission of the Chan school, donned the monastic robes and immediately applied himself to his family’s ancestral vocation,
studying the *Sifen Vinaya*. Subsequently, wishing to distance himself from the Dharma to achieve personal purification, he took up his staff and traveled south.
While traveling to investigate the fundamental tenets of the Western Tradition, he arrived at Jia Shan. He stayed with him for a long time at Daolin Monastery.

When the old monk was appointed to lead Jiangshan, [the Master] continued his inquiries with even greater persistence. It became clear that he had mastered the ability to cast off intellectual understanding;

he sought to penetrate directly through the total functioning of the mind. In every response and verse he composed according to circumstances, he proceeded with directness and decisiveness, possessing a profound depth of character that was truly admirable. However—

With this faculty, one should further apply oneself with diligence and resolve. Reaching the ultimate depths, there is no depth; reaching the ultimate subtlety, there is no subtlety. It is a great rest, a great stability.
Without stirring so much as a speck of dust, one simply maintains this state of leisurely ease. Neither sages nor ordinary beings can fathom it.
Only when the myriad virtues have not been brought forward can the dharma-kāṣāya be entrusted.

Yantou said: "To reject things is superior; to pursue things is inferior. Whether it be the myriad realms and conditions, the teachings of the past and present, or responding with adaptability to the immediate situation—if one's own fundamental footing is empty, still, perfectly luminous, and tranquil illumination, then whatever comes to disturb me...
If one can wield the precious sword of the Vajra King at the vanguard to sever [all obstacles], then with a majestic and awe-inspiring presence, one will decisively cut off everything;
without waiting for them to retreat, they will withdraw of their own accord. Is this not to have ample leisure and ease?

Should one’s fundamental grounding be unclear and one fall into even slight hesitation, then one will be dragged along and pulled away, unable to distinguish or separate oneself from the situation. How could one avoid being turned by external conditions?
Once you have followed him away, you will ultimately have no share of freedom. The Way is simple and easy; it consists only in turning back and following along.
Those who skillfully embody the Way should reflect deeply upon this.

For the sake of this one matter, the ancients were driven to such an extent that they would abandon their entire bodies, stand in the snow, carry mortars on their backs, or sell their hearts and livers.
Casting both arms into a mass of raging fire, having his seven limbs cut and sliced to feed tigers, sacrificing his head and giving away his eyes—
these and hundreds of other such deeds demonstrate that unless one undergoes hardship, one cannot reach profound realization. Those of noble ambition should surely take the ancients as their peers,
looking up to Yan Hui and admiring the legacy of Lin Xiangru.

Great masters of the school have attained liberation through both favorable and adverse conditions; they cultivate a resolve and vision such that they would rather grind their bones to powder than retreat.
They seek the great rather than the trivial, and the distant rather than the near, facing a thousand hardships and myriad sufferings as difficult and perilous as a silver mountain or an iron wall.
In this state, cast off the body, relinquish life, and let go with both hands to take up this great matter of cause and condition.

Severing attachments and departing from views, bring to rest the frantic mechanism of karmic consciousness. Open the gate of Great Liberation and resolve the great matter of one’s own birth and death, thereby fulfilling the original vow of the initial aspiration.
Regard the six sense organs, the four elements, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, and the seven elements as they truly are.

Like wildflowers in the void that arise and perish in confusion, [all phenomena] are nothing but the total inheritance of the inconceivable, fundamental essence of the Buddhas and patriarchs—vast, empty, quiescent, and profoundly lucid, the adamantine true body.

With its roots deeply established and its stillness perfected, even if one raises a single hair, a speck of dust, a single gesture, or a single phrase for a mere moment, there is nothing that does not emerge from within this fundamental source. Although it is called "Great," it is so.
The great functioning of the pivot has already been a chaotic muddle; it has already been grasped and felt.

Where else could one apply the mind, apply nature, apply the mysterious, apply the wondrous, apply principle, or apply phenomena? Reaching this point is like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace.

Even hearing of Chan and the Way, erasing their traces and swallowing one's voice, is not yet the ultimate limit—how much less so the remaining shadows and lights, forms and sounds, mountains, rivers, and the great earth!
The earth, dewdrops, pillars, and lanterns—seen by the eyes and heard by the ears—are like those who shoulder the cangue and embrace the shackles.
Have you not seen how Deshan would strike one upon entering the gate, and Linji would shout upon entering the gate? This is the "ready-made case" of Muzhou. Look closely at this:
he has already entered the mud and the water with a most earnest, compassionate heart. Therefore it is said: "If one were to exclusively exalt the teachings and the school... [the Dharma...]
The hall floor must have grass one zhang deep; as for the other expedient means regarding doors and eaves, know that these were done out of necessity and by constraint.
These are all acts of compassion and the mobilization of pity by the great *kalyāṇamitras* of old, serving as monuments for future generations.
It enables those of noble resolve to reach the point where their realization is indestructible and they are radiant from all sides;

not only does this benefit themselves, but it also benefits others, transmitting the lamp of infinity and continuing the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom. From the Tang dynasty, through the Five Dynasties, until the beginning of our present dynasty.
Bearing heavy burdens and aspiring to occupy the ancestral seat, they gallop like dragons and tigers, rushing south and north.
How many are there who pull out wedges and nails for others, ungluing the sticky and untying the bonds? It is not that there are none in recent times;

This may cause the supreme, wondrous, and lofty great function of the Patriarchs to nearly perish.

Fortunately, there are still later descendants who transcend their peers and stand apart from the common crowd, who match those of antiquity, disregarding right and wrong, gain and loss, self and other, and acceptance and rejection, resolving matters with a heart of iron and stone.
With a resolve that cannot be rolled back nor shifted, one should endure austerity and plain food, undaunted by hardships, and press forward in investigation.
In this way, one may inherit the fragrant traces and continue the lofty style of past generations, serving as a bright torch for humanity and as the sun and moon for the dark alleys of ignorance.
This has been my constant private aspiration. Now that I am filled with indignation and resolve to bring it forth, it is vital that I carry this through from beginning to end.
I must seek out a master upon the sea who possesses the means to kill without batting an eye, so as to strip away [all delusions] once and for all;
thus, not only will I repay my own transcendent original mind, but I shall also extend a hand within the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma.
Moreover, this gate transcends the distinction between self and other and is free from love and hatred; it values only right knowledge and right view.
How could it matter whose son one is? Since we are all equally under the lineage of Caoxi, what room is there for distinctions such as "that sect" or "this school" among us?

It is like when Zhaozhou asked Qinglin, "What is the Buddha? He replied, "A child of the fire element comes seeking fire. He then—

Turning the light back upon oneself, one no longer commits evil and understands evil as such; at that very moment, it is like obtaining a lamp in the darkness or finding treasure in poverty.
How could this be a small matter? If one truly and sincerely believes this, for thousands of millions of kalpas one shall long enjoy its benefits.
Therefore, the Way is fundamentally wordless, yet the Way is revealed through words. If one attains this Way, it is by no means dependent on words and phrases. Hereafter, as soon as there is...

Among the great masters of the past, none failed to pass through this training ground, being polished and refined therein before they were fit to practice and uphold the Way. However...
