It is precisely here that you should swiftly cut through. After long practice until it is pure and mature, there will be no difference between you and those such as Vimalakīrti or the Elder Pang.
An Exhortation to Goodness for the Purpose of Awakening the Nature of Minister Hu:
At the very heels of every person, there originally exists this great radiance—empty, penetrating, and spiritually resonant—which is called the "glory of one's original ground.

Before the emergence of Buddhas or sentient beings, it was perfectly interfused and boundless, residing within one’s own heart-mind (*cunzhong*). It is the source of the four elements and the five [aggregates].
The master of the aggregates is, from the beginning, free of defilement and its nature is tranquil and still.

It is only because of deluded thoughts that suddenly arise as veils and obstructions that it is bound by the six faculties and the six sense objects, resulting in the mutual adhesion and clinging of faculty and object.
Thus, one grasps at all objective realms and gives rise to all deluded thoughts, wallowing in the toil of birth and death without attaining liberation. For this reason, the Buddhas and Patriarchs...

The Master realized this true source and penetrated its fundamental nature. Out of compassion for those mired in the depths of samsara, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion and appeared in the world precisely for this purpose.
The Western arrival of Bodhidharma and his "separate transmission outside the teachings" were also for this very reason.

It is simply a matter of those with great capacity and sharp intelligence turning the light back upon themselves to reflect; they must clearly awaken to this mind at the point where not a single thought arises. How much more so regarding this mind!
It can give rise to all mundane and supramundane dharmas. For a long time, it has been firmly sealed within the square inch of the heart-mind, solitary and towering, alive and agile.
As soon as the mind gives rise to a thought or a movement of consciousness, this original luminosity is immediately obscured. If you now wish to penetrate it directly and easily:
Simply let go and allow the body and mind to become empty and weary; they are void yet numinous, still yet illuminating. Internally, forget self-view;
externally, sever even the slightest speck of dust. When the internal and external are transparently clear, there is only the single reality.

The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena, are all established in dependence upon the "Other. This "Other" is able to penetrate and transcend such myriad conditions. And...
All such myriad conditions originally lack any fixed characteristics; they exist solely by relying on the transformation of this light.
If one can truly believe in and attain this single plot of ground, then by knowing one thing, all things are known; by clarifying one thing, all things are clarified.
Thus, whatever actions one performs will all be the ultimate, bottomless, great liberation—the adamantine true essence itself. One must first awaken to and realize this.
Only after [establishing] the mind should one cultivate all forms of goodness. Have you not seen how Bai Juyi asked Niaoke, "What is the Way?
Niaoke replied, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Bai said, "Even a three-year-old child can say this.
Niaoke said, "Though a three-year-old child can say it, an eighty-year-old man cannot practice it. Therefore, one should investigate and transcend the correct.

One must practice with the eyes and feet assisting one another. If one can refrain from all evils and diligently cultivate various virtues, even a person who merely observes the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths will not fall into ruin;

how much more so for one who first awakens to the wondrously luminous true mind and its firm, correct essence, and subsequently practices according to their capacity, performing various good deeds to ensure that all people do not become deluded.
Regarding cause and effect: know that the causes for hell and heaven are all created by one's own fundamental mind.
You should maintain this mind with equanimity—without self or others, without love or hatred, without grasping or rejecting, and without gain or loss. Gradually nurture it for thirty or twenty years;
when you encounter circumstances that are favorable or adverse, you will attain non-retrogression. Upon reaching the threshold of birth and death, you will naturally become carefree and unburdened.
Regarding all such fears: the principle requires sudden enlightenment, while practice must necessarily be gradual.

I have often observed those who study the Buddha’s teachings who rely solely on their worldly intelligence and eloquence to snatch at marvelous phrases from the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, using them as handles for conversation to display their skill and understanding.
This is not right view; it should be abandoned. One ought to settle the mind in stillness, forgetting all external conditions.

Investigate thoroughly until you reach a state of ultimate, transparent clarity. Then, drawing forth [the truth] from within your own priceless and inexhaustible treasure trove, how could there be anything that is not real?
However, you must first awaken to your original nature and clearly perceive the true essence of "mind itself is Buddha.
Free yourself from all delusive conditions so that you become spontaneously serene and pure; only then should you practice all manner of wholesome deeds and give rise to the Great...
Compassion benefits sentient beings; whatever one does is entirely equal, selfless, and unattached. Wondrous wisdom is manifested, penetrating the fundamental essence.
How marvelous is such skillful conduct! Thus it is said: "If you simply possess the heart of resolve, you will certainly not be deceived.
Take awakening as your standard and do not lament its being late. Be careful.

I show this to you, Academician Zhang Xuānjī, one of the most profoundly realized among the great scholars: this single, supreme, and uniquely liberating point of the secret transmission is the ultimate in brevity and essentiality.
It requires nothing more than a sharp faculty and superior wisdom for the capacities of teacher and student to meet, so that one may directly grasp it at once. When will such a time come?

Whether it be the ascending and descending of Xuanyan, the profound subtlety of the rational nature, the primary and secondary, the host and guest, or the functions of speech and action—as soon as one gives rise to conceptual understanding, one is immediately bound and fettered, leaving no room for freedom.

Therefore, a true master of the fundamental division never steps onto another's fishing hook nor falls into another's snare; they only illuminate and realize through their own inner clarity, leaving not even a hair’s breadth lingering in the breast.

Transcendent and solitary, he does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion, nor does he share a dwelling with the thousand sages. He is liberated, pure, and pristine, profoundly still and empty yet coalescent.
When it comes to engaging with conditions and responding to capacities, he is like a whirling sword or a mass of fierce fire—how can one approach him?
Speech and silence, existence and non-existence, movement and stillness, self and other—all are cut off at once. Therefore, the Way [is found in] the very last word.
The phrase first reaches the sturdy barrier; it seizes the vital ford, allowing passage neither to ordinary beings nor to sages.

Having no other choice, it is called "the single phrase," called "the true state," called "the crown of the head," and called "the Vajra King. As soon as one grasps this meaning, all becomes distinct and transparently penetrating;
emotional defilements, conceptual thoughts, views, and intellectual wisdom naturally dissolve. In that moment, time becomes vast and expansive, and one attains great self-mastery.

Abiding in this, one cultivates the self and conducts oneself; by this, one stabilizes the state and secures the realm. Its bounty reaches all living beings, while one's status and reputation grow ever more exalted and the workings of the mind become increasingly upright.
Yet, one is able to not dwell upon these achievements and not claim these virtues. For ten thousand ages it is but a single moment; for ten thousand years it is but a single thought.
The ten directions are as if witnessed firsthand; creation is held within the palm of the hand. It is simply a matter of turning things around and returning to heaven.
To take Mount Sumeru and place it within a mustard seed, or to cast the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters—how could this be difficult?

Having already attained profound realization, one should further refine it through practice, so that power may increase effortlessly and the mind remain in tranquil, great samādhi. This shall not merely exhaust this present life;
throughout the bounds of the future, there shall be nothing that does not rely upon this. When meeting fellow practitioners who share the same realization, one need not even raise [the subject].
If one knows that there is a resonance beyond words, it may be appropriate to set this aside and not discuss it further. The *Biographies* state: "The Tathāgata has secret words;
Kāśyapa did not conceal them. It is precisely because Kāśyapa alone was able to not conceal them that they are called "secret."

The lay practitioner Fu Shen, who shares the same shrine [with me], is a scholar-official whom many encounter when they discuss the nature of reality (*li-xing*). His understanding is relatively close to the fundamental source;

his broad knowledge encompasses the profound and mysterious, penetrating the interface between heaven and humanity, and harmonizing the Three Teachings. As a versatile Confucian (*tong-ru*), he has composed writings with the desire that they be transmitted.
They are called people of different generations. Do they perhaps reflect upon their own conduct and establish principles? Or do they withdraw to listen and cultivate the deeds of the worthy?

Some have fallen into superficiality, seeking only to browse through texts to provide material for conversation; others value words and delight in victory, using them to subdue their peers and increase their own views (*asmimāna*).

None of these are correct causes. Though such people may be superior to those who are utterly ignorant and lack faith and orientation, they nevertheless harbor slander based on their own solitary views and shallow learning.

Alas! Those who obscure the fruit and are deluded regarding the cause fall into the stream of worldly convention. Yet, compared to them, those who are sincere in their pursuit of truth, purify themselves, undergo rigorous austerity, retreat from ambition, and forget their own selves to achieve realization;
who tread upon solid ground, penetrate the sensory roots and objects, and transcend all artifice—such as the Great Being Vimalakīrti and the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada—are truly their peers.
They have fully realized the fruits of the Way, transcending both the mundane and the supramundane.

For instance, there were the Prime Minister Pei Xiu, Grand Master Lu Xun, Minister Chen Cao, Attendant Wang Jing, Li Xizhi of Xiangyang, Zheng Yu, and Wei Zhou during the Tang dynasty—none of whom failed to investigate with their whole hearts and, throughout their lives, attained the full utilization of our school.

They were especially profound in clarifying the manifestations of the Dharma, reaching its depths and exhausting its most abstruse mysteries. So too were the Imperial Secretary Yang Dainian and the Prince Consort Li.
The Commandant may now drive side by side with Master Pang; indeed, he possesses great power and capacity.

While on the path of official service, he did not abandon his position as a magistrate, yet he wandered beyond the mundane world, grasping the very core of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, forging the minds of worldly people, and exercising the integration of secular and sacred affairs.

Emerging from amidst the ranks of court officials, he served as a regional governor and acted as an inner and outer protector for the Great Master. Is this not the result of his long-standing [merit]?
Having received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) at Mount Ling, you have developed the vows and practices refined through hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes to manifest such karmic conditions.
Although the Buddha-dharma has become diluted in recent times, there are still a great many among the noble gentry who possess deep faith;

they truly possess an ancient style. It must be said that these individuals constitute half of the three superior classes [of practitioners]. If one aspires to this path, one must surely strive for the highest level.
You of great capacity, do not measure yourself as being of middling or inferior capacity; then it will not be difficult to transcend the mundane and emerge from the dust to attain great liberation.
It requires only single-mindedness and long-term perseverance. When encountering adverse conditions or evil objects, cut them off directly and decisively. As it is said:
"Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of your head, your perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom shall never be lost."
When Li Bo, the Shiyi (Court Reminder), was serving as Governor of Jiujiang, he encountered Gui Zong at Shiyian; they were struck by mutual affinity upon their first meeting.
One day, Li Bo suddenly asked, "In the teachings it is said that a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru—is there such a principle?
Gui Zong replied, "Is it not true what people say, that you are Li Wanjuan? Li Bo answered, "Indeed. Zong then said, "I observe that your physical stature does not even fill three feet."
"Where shall ten thousand scrolls of books be placed? Li immediately grasped the meaning. How could this be discussed with those who cling to appearances, harbor attachments, and guard fixed views?
This requires a capacity that, by following the finger, sees the moon; and by forgetting the trap, catches the fish or rabbit.
Only such a person may disregard the nesting place of expedient means. They must know the point of arrival in a single stroke, and only then emerge with brilliant clarity.
Having reached a place where the seven paths meet and the eight roads converge, one manifests great enjoyment.
When Han Yu asked Master Dadian: "I, Yu, am burdened by the complexities of official duties; I pray that you, Master, will grant me a single word on the essential points of the Buddha-dharma."
Dianzhi remained sitting rigidly, appearing utterly bewildered. At that time, Sanping was standing in attendance; he struck the meditation seat once and said, "Minister, the Master said:
'First, move them with concentration; afterwards, uproot them with wisdom. Minister Wen was greatly delighted and said, "The Chan Master’s Dharma is steep and precipitous;
yet, through his attendant, there is a point of entry. One of such sharp faculties and spiritual lineage requires but a single nudge."
Thus it proceeds. Observe how this master and his disciple employ skillful means toward that which is ineffable and inexpressible, bringing it forth.

Were it not for Han Gong’s keen intelligence, how could he have grasped this? As the saying goes, the one who wields the axe must have a nimble hand, but the one who receives the blow must also possess a substance that remains unmoved;
only then do both enter the sublime. Otherwise, it results in nothing but a display of clumsy blunders.
It is so. Observe this Nanyue: day after day he entered the hall, and morning after morning he sought instruction.

Therefore, when the man of old beckoned him from across the river with a fan, he immediately strode across and took it to heart. Now, to write such things down on paper and ink is to knowingly commit an offense.
Shi Huang Shengshu: "When meeting, do not bring it up; as soon as you intend to speak, one already knows it exists. To examine this closely is already to wade through water and drag through mud;

how much more so for all other complications? Thus, within the realm of a person of thorough understanding, it is fitting that it be steep and absolute—how could any entanglement be tolerated? This is because...
This one person alone is permitted to be carefree and unencumbered. Yet, though one may move with the speed of lightning or a shooting star, one cannot avoid missing the mark.

To simply raise such a realization in this manner is an offense that fills the heavens. If you can directly comprehend it at the moment before meeting [the teacher] or before a single thought arises—this depends entirely upon the individual.
Do not further attempt to manifest patterns or produce intellectual interpretations. Take care, take care!
When the former Court Attendant Monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.

This became a model for those who inquire throughout the world; yet there are many who produce divergent interpretations. Only those who penetrate directly, without relying on anything [external], [truly grasp it].

If you act with intellectual understanding, you will immediately suffer the consequences. As soon as there is even a hair’s breadth of a "view" that pricks you, everything becomes a pitch-black expanse.
Have you not seen how Fayen raised the question to Jue Tiezui? Is it not true that Zhaozhou has the saying, "The cypress tree in the courtyard"? Is it not so?
"Master Jueyun, do not slander the former master; the former master never spoke such words. Simply investigate in this manner, for this is precisely where the ancients were direct."
Venerable Yanyang asked Zhaozhou, “What is it like when one brings nothing at all? Zhaozhou said, “Put it down.
Yanyang said, “Since I bring nothing at all, what is there to put down? Zhaozhou said, “I see that you cannot let go.
Thereupon, Yanyang attained great enlightenment. Later, Master Nan composed a verse which says: “When one brings nothing at all, two...”
Carrying it on one's shoulders, one cannot lift it up; yet, in the moment of these words, one suddenly realizes one’s error. Within the heart, joy is boundless;
once malice and evil are cast from the mind, even snakes and tigers become one’s true friends. For a thousand or ten thousand years, this pure wind has not ceased. But try for yourself:
when you frequently attempt to lift something up, how is it when nothing at all comes forth? The Master said, "Put it down. Suddenly, realization is not difficult to attain. Thus spoke the Monk.
I asked Yunmen, "If one does not give rise to a single thought, is there still transgression? Yunmen replied, "Mount Sumeru. This, too, is direct and essential.
With no affairs, keep the mind empty and contemplate in stillness; apply yourself to the basic practice and simply continue to hold it up for inspection.
After a long time, you will naturally find the point of entry.
When Master Lü showed the story of the First Patriarch Bodhidharma arriving in the Liang dynasty and meeting Emperor Wu, he applied it directly with a single stroke upon the crown of the head.
Yet Emperor Wu did not offer his recommendation; this has caused people to wring their hands in frustration to this day.

How many who came after have waded through the mud and water, following his footprints to speculate and construct hundreds of thousands of divergent interpretations? Yet they have never even dreamed of him;
they merely produce one expedient condition from another expedient condition, and give rise to one view from another view. Therefore it is said: "The sword has gone far away."

This is like carving a mark on a boat [after it has already sailed away]. Had one been able at that time to cut off this "Hu" and "Han," one would not have fallen into the trap of dragging others down.
As it is said, "Only by knowing gratitude can one repay it. But how, pray tell, can one cut it off?
To Su Zhonghu, Governor of Shu: The Great Dharma is fundamentally ordinary.
It lies in being sharp-witted, diligent, and broad-minded; it is not by acting as if one were exceptionally clever that one enters it easily.

When all things are equalized and the mind itself is utterly ungraspable, it vanishes of its own accord. Thus, the original nature is perfectly luminous and spontaneously complete, requiring no artificial effort.
It is a profound realization that cuts off the stream, a state where there is neither excess nor deficiency; this is the essential pivot of natural spontaneity. This is what is meant by the saying:
"The moment you touch the palm of your hand, it is decided. You should cause this to be constantly manifest during the course of daily life. How could it be otherwise?
It is not that they were not profoundly settled. The ancients awakened to the mind; they awakened to this very mind. They triggered the mechanism;

they triggered this very mechanism. Thus, it remains unshakable for ten thousand generations. One simply maintains this state of leisurely ease, transcending and attaining it alone, with no further duality.
If there were duality, then two things would stand opposed; then there would be self and other, gain and loss. One cannot truly set foot upon the solid ground and advance a single step further.

When not a single dharma is established through even a step, one then settles into a state of clarity and perceives the person of original nature. One discards the objects within the breast and loses the karmic triggers before the eyes.
Thus, one attains a state of total stability, forever free from regression, and gains the skillful means of fearlessness by which to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
It is essential that this be maintained for a long duration, in continuous succession without interruption, for it to be truly effective.

Shown to Grand Marshal Huang:

This Way is profound and secluded, reaching to the point where heaven and earth had not yet taken form and before the distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas arose. It is a state of profound stillness and silence, the root of all transformations.
From the beginning, it is neither existent nor non-existent; it does not fall into the conditions of worldly dust. Radiant and brilliant, its limits are unfathomable. It is—non-existent.
There is no reality that can be realized, and no subtlety that can be perfected. It dwells transcendentally beyond the realm of form and thought; there is nothing by which it may be compared.

Therefore, the Perfected Person alone realizes this state of sharp detachment, becoming utterly still and pure. Having penetrated this profound source, they directly and abruptly extract the essence through the power of skillful means to meet those of the highest capacity, establishing no gradual stages.
For this reason, it is called the "School of the Lineage" (Zongcheng) and the "Teaching Outside the Scriptures" (Jiaowai).
Acting apart from conventional practice, he seals everything with the Single Seal, thereby turning the pivot so that there is no room for deliberation.

Whether it be the plucking of a flower and the smile, the tossing of a needle or the raising of a whisk, leaning on a staff or resting against a desk, or the twinkling of an eye and the lifting of a brow—all emerge from the nest and den.

The principles and the path are spread across the road of speech like sparks struck from stone or flashes of lightning; they are sudden and swift, undergoing ten thousand transformations and a thousand shifts in an instant.
Never having relied on anything, one must penetrate to the very top and bottom, severing all nets and cages. This is permitted only for those of brilliant capacity, not for the dull-witted;
it requires the very air of one who possesses the resolve to kill without batting an eye. To realize everything at once, to clarify everything through a single clarity.
Thereafter, they penetrate directly, severing death and giving birth to life, transcending the mundane and entering the sacred.
Possessing profound vision and lofty discernment, they do not reveal their sharp edges in ordinary circumstances; yet when they emerge casually, they startle the multitudes and move the masses.

This is because their roots are deep and their foundation is firm, having pierced through to the void beyond the kalpa prior to King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda, which is no different and no distinct from the functioning of this very day. Being thus able to act...

Possessing great power, he is capable of bearing heavy burdens and traveling far; having attained great mastery, he can condense three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* into a single thought-moment and expand seven days into an eon—all of which are but minor feats of his activity.
How much more so when he casts the Great Trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters and contains Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed;
this is merely his daily fare. Formerly, Prime Minister Pei attained the essential meaning from Huangbo. Yang Da...
Nian received the seal from Guanghui; Vimalakīrti grasped the world of Abhirati with his hand; the old man Pang sucked the Western River in a single gulp—how could these be difficult matters?
It is simply a matter of directly apprehending this great causal nexus. Since one already possesses this foundation of the Way, [there is nothing further to seek].

At all times, one must not allow others to dictate one's actions. Briefly speaking, when facing the moment of responding to commands and calls, one must fix the eyes and employ swift mechanisms and sharp intelligence to turn all phenomena back toward oneself.

If one can thus master the principles of expansion and contraction, release and capture, how could this differ from the great masters of old who embraced the Way, accumulated virtue, and were thoroughly proficient in their practice?

"How can there be going within change? He replied, "Going itself does not change.
Were it not for having trodden upon the ground of reality, how could one penetrate to such a depth? How could this be measured by mere words or intellectual thought?

It is because one has practiced until reaching the ultimate depth, arriving at a state free from leakage, that one cannot be confined or contained. For those who study the Way, their resolve must lie beyond [the mundane].
When the physical form dies, birth and death are merged, and past and present are transcended, severing all coming and going.
One must strive to reach the upper stream and penetrate the ultimate realm of the True Dharma—profound, deep, and subtle. One must settle oneself, becoming as clear and pure as white dew;

not a single thread of conceptual thought should fall into the conditions of worldly dust. Directly, the mind should be like withered wood or rotten stumps, like a great dead man without a breath of life. The mind...
The mind is devoid of cognition; its moments of thought abide nowhere. Even if a thousand sages were to appear, they could not shift or alter it.

Thus, one may cause flowers to bloom upon withered wood, manifesting great potential and giving rise to great function, exercising compassion and extending pity. This is the function of no-effort and the action of no-action;
how could it fall within the realm of gain and loss, right and wrong? To allow even a single hair’s breadth of attachment is to encounter resistance in the midst of life.
The realm of death. How can one who has not yet crossed over oneself deliver others? The Great Being Vimalakīrti does not abide in the stage of the Golden Grain;
he enters wine shops and brothels to perform the great liberating Buddha-work.
To show Master Wei Xueshi:

they are presented face-to-face, and at that very moment, they are already divided into ten parts. If one possesses sharp faculties, a single word of realization would already be a state of utter ruin;
how much more so when one resorts to paper and ink, engaging in verbal explanations to lay out a path—this only becomes increasingly remote. Nevertheless, this passage...

The great conditions are fully present within every person; simply seek them within yourself and do not look for them elsewhere. For one's own mind is signless, empty, leisurely, still, and profoundly secret, eternally and ever-present.
It seals and stabilizes the six sense-faculties and the four elements, its radiance swallowing all phenomena like a host of elephants.

If both mind and objects are simultaneously stilled and forgotten, transcending all cognition and views and departing from all intellectual understanding, then to penetrate directly through this is itself the Buddha-mind. Beyond this, there is nothing more.

There is not a single dharma. Therefore, when the Patriarch came from the West, he spoke only of directly pointing to the human mind, of a separate transmission outside the teachings, and of the singular transmission of the true seal.
He did not establish words or phrases, intending for people to find rest in the present moment.

If you give rise to thoughts or stir your mind, identifying with objects or views, playing with the vital spirit, or clinging to conceptual nests, then there is no connection at all. Shishuang said: "Rest."
Go to rest! Go until mold grows upon your lips; go as a single white silk ribbon; go for ten thousand years in a single thought; go cold and still;
go like an incense burner in an ancient temple. Simply believe these words and practice accordingly.
Relax the body and mind so they are like earth, wood, stone, or a clod of dirt, until you reach a state of non-perception, non-cognition, and immovability.

Relying on this instruction, let the breath cease and all mental entanglements fall away; when not a single thought arises, there is a sudden joy, like finding a lamp in the dark or a treasure for the poor.
The four elements and five aggregates become light and at ease, as if a heavy burden has been cast off. Body and mind suddenly open up in clarity, illuminating everything.
When all marks are realized to be like flowers in the sky and are thus ungraspable, this original face appears; the natural splendor of the fundamental ground is revealed.
This single path of pure emptiness is precisely one’s own place of resting the body and relinquishing life—a state of ease, non-action, and joy.
All the myriad sutras and treatises speak of nothing but this. The functions, skillful means, and wondrous gates of the sages of the past and the sages of the future are solely this.

This refers to it. It is like using a key to open the lock of a treasure trove; once the door is opened, the myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences encountered at every turn and through every circumstance are none other than the wondrous treasures that naturally belong to one's own fundamental portion. Whatever is grasped with the hand can be utilized;
this is called "once attained, forever attained" throughout the bounds of the future. It is attained within non-attainment, yet even this attainment is not [ultimately real].
To attain it is indeed to truly attain it. If it were not so, one would fall into a semblance of *prajñā* that involves having something to realize or attain, which is ultimately incomplete.
Once you have suddenly and clearly realized this fundamental ground, you may then exert effort and properly engage in practice.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, you must diligently tread the path, neither grasping at a single dharma nor rejecting a single one.
The Dharma is perfectly interfused in its own place; every place is this samādhi, and every dust mote is the Patriarch.
Yet, one does not harbor a mind of superior attachment, but practices exclusively the Great Way of the single mark of equality—without person and without self.

One upholds the precepts and observes the fasts, diligently cultivating the three karmas until they are pure and untainted, like a drop of water or a frozen drop of ice. Thus, each of the six perfections and ten thousand practices is brought to full completion.
Penetrating [the truth], one awakens the great potential and initiates the great function, successively causing all people to believe in this, investigate this, and realize this.

One must ensure that practice and understanding correspond; be careful not to harbor the demonic and heterodox views of nihilism—recklessly denying cause and effect and wandering aimlessly in vacuity.
To do so even for a moment is to slander Prajñāpāramitā and invite evil retribution. Therefore, the Buddhas and Patriarchs established the teachings, calling it "clarity."

Pure and Bright Instruction: One must rely upon this primary cause before one can realize the wondrous fruit. All the power of a lifetime is precisely for the purpose of penetrating and transcending birth and death.

If one realizes perfect enlightenment in a single thought-moment and practices in every thought-moment, then by practicing through non-practice and acting through non-action, one refines and grinds oneself forward.
Thus, amidst all circumstances, one neither clings nor attaches, and is not led astray by the wholesome...
Bound by the conditions of evil karma, one attains great liberation. After a hundred years have passed, one is suddenly and alone liberated; the path ahead is bright and clear.
From kalpa to kalpa and birth to birth, one never loses sight of one's own nature. This is to be "thoroughly finished and completely settled.

All of this reveals the essence of the profound and wondrous state that does not fall into verbal expression. One should contemplate with a darkened mind and investigate deeply, so as to penetrate through worldly toil and realize purity.
This is the pure and wondrous fruit.

It reveals that the virtuous and noble person is entirely Buddha, and the Buddha is entirely the person; when person and Buddha are without distinction, one has truly attained the Way. This is the ultimate truth.

This is what is meant. However, when the mind is true, both person and Buddha are true. For this reason, the Patriarchs pointed directly to the human mind alone, so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha.
Although this mind is fully possessed by every person, from time immemorial it has been pure and unstained.
From the beginning, there was no grasping or attachment; quiescent illumination was凝然 (stagnant/immutable), utterly devoid of subject and object, perfectly complete as a full, round sphere.

It was solely because one failed to maintain one's own nature and gave rise to a single moment of deluded movement that boundless views and knowledge arose, causing one to drift through the various realms of existence.

At the very root of one's feet, this fundamental radiance has been constantly worn like a pendant, never having been obscured; yet, regarding the sense organs and their objects, one has needlessly suffered entanglement and bondage. If...

Able to preserve their fundamental faculties from past lives, when they encounter the Buddhas, the Patriarchs, or the Masters, at the point where these teachers provide direct and immediate instruction, they instantly cast off their greasy monastic robes.
Standing forth entirely naked and bare, they directly assume responsibility for this reality. It does not come from without, nor does it emerge from within;
in that very moment, they realize this nature with vast clarity. What more need be said of the "minds of humans and Buddhas"? It is like casting [a metal object] onto a red-hot furnace.
A single speck of snow. Where else could there be so much distress? For this reason, this school does not establish written words or phrases;

it permits only those of the highest vehicle’s faculties to realize and witness the essence directly—like a whirling wind, a swift thunderclap, a flash of lightning, or a shooting star—severing the stream of birth and death, shattering the shell of ignorance, and attaining immediate, sudden clarity without the slightest doubt. II.

Throughout the six periods of the day, all circumstances and conditions are transformed into supreme, wondrous wisdom. Why, then, should one seek stillness by wearying oneself with noise, or abandon the former to grasp the latter?
When the One is true, all is true; when the One is fully realized, all is fully realized. All phenomena are subsumed within the source of the mind.
Holding the mechanism of power beyond the mundane world, he manifests forms in response to phenomena such that no dharma is not perfected. What, then, could exist as a separate "self"?
One must first settle upon one's own true footing; once the position is firmly established, it is natural for the wind to blow and the grass to bow.
This is why Master Wang was able to manage his livelihood from the age of eighteen, while Xianglin required forty years to do so.

They form a single whole. Those who are bound by worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata. It depends solely upon the person to skillfully observe the wind and set the sails.
With every thought continuing in succession and every mind remaining non-abiding, one walks the path of eternal life.

Thus, one shares the same virtue, the same essence, the same actions, and the same realization as the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Moreover, the governance of a hundred *li* rests entirely in one’s hands; how much more so the task of pacifying the people!
Benefiting others is itself one’s own peace. The myriad transformations share this single mechanism; the thousand differences are unified by this single illumination.
Even the entire dharma-realm, as vast as the atoms within all lands, can be harmoniously integrated—how much more so the fact that there is no difference between humans and Buddhas?
The late Master Shifang Qing remarked:

"When the Venerable Bodhidharma came from Central India, how could he have ever carried a single thing with him? Yet when he traveled through Liang and Wei and sat facing the wall at Shaolin, no one recognized him.
Only Huiké showed diligent devotion, standing in the snow and severing his arm, until the Master finally began to show a slight measure of compassion. It was because of this that..."
It is precisely the mind. If you say that words have no way to enter, it is like saying that even if one speaks, what can be said to such a person?
You should know that only such a person can fully comprehend this and remain free from leakage.
Therefore, to enter this gate, one must possess sharp faculties and be able to swiftly cast aside all prior views and intellectual pathways, leaving the breast empty.
Exertion does not remain for even a hair’s breadth; it is a transparent illumination of the void and the concentrated, where the paths of speech and thought are cut off.

One directly accords with the original source, merging into boundless stillness. When one spontaneously attains that which is inherently present—the wondrous state of non-attainment—only then can it be called "faith reaching its limit" and "vision being thoroughly penetrated.

Yet, there still exists an immeasurable, boundless, unfathomable, and incalculable great capacity and great function. If one were to retain even a trace of subject and object, one would fall into the dust of conditioned phenomena.
Thus, it would ultimately fail to correspond with the urgent [need]. For this reason, the ancient masters exhorted us to "directly set down" and "rest.
This section is like a swift falcon or hawk that pierces the clouds, breaks through the sun, and soars past the wind and the thickets; it is direct and admits no room for deliberation.
If one hesitates, one has already missed the mark. From this, it can be known that this constitutes the "separate transmission outside the teachings."
Since you already have this aspiration, I ask that you let go and take full responsibility for your own being;
then all things will manifest as they are, and the First Patriarch never came, nor did you yourself attain anything.
To Li Yifu: This Way is the most direct and essential; it does not go beyond a single word. Yet this word was not proclaimed from the Buddha’s own mouth, nor was it spoken by the patriarchs.

If one were to say that "the very mind is not the mind" or "the very Buddha is not the Buddha," then one would be like someone marking the boat to find a lost sword or waiting for a rabbit to goring a stump—utterly devoid of true engagement.

If one were to silently comprehend these words, how could they ever fall from the lips? Those who chase after clods of earth have thus engaged in groundless conjecture, claiming that even a blink or a movement has not been glimpsed in their dreams.

They fail to realize that the structural principles and sequential steps transmitted from of old are not for the purpose of establishing cleverness or views and knowledge, nor are they a discourse on the provisional and the real, or the realms of illumination and function. Being left with no other recourse, I shall now set them forth according to the text.
Below the cloud-heads, staff and shouts fly back and forth like shooting stars and flashing lightning. Those of superior capacity understand their point of fall upon merely hearing them.
But what, after all, is that one word? Is it the "cypress tree," the "Mount Sumeru," the "exposed nakedness," or the "universal delusion"?
Is it the "board-carrying fellow" who, having been scrutinized through, is told to "go drink tea"? I dare say, elder brother, you have understood. Take care.
To say, "I have not yet penetrated; let me go rest" or "let me go attend the hall," is merely to be a spirit clinging to the grass or perching on the wood.
Some say, "It is so. To claim that the Patriarch took the Buddha’s words on the mind as his school and "no-gate" as his dharma-gate is to mistake the zero-point on the scale.
You must wait until the bottom of the bucket falls out, like waking from a dream, achieving great penetration and great awakening; only then...
One can indeed take this statement to heart.

In showing the essential point for transcending to Master Han, the Prefectural Commissioner, [the Master] said that it lies solely in resting the mind. As soon as mental perceptions and views arise, one moves further away; therefore, one must rest directly and immediately until reaching the state of total cessation.

In this ground of no-mind, all is empty, leisurely, and tranquil. Though there be ten thousand transformations and a thousand turns, they are neither external nor internal; they do not interfere with one another at all.
Naturally surging and flowing, responding freely and without fixed direction, one can thereby master the twelve hours of the day and employ all dharmas.
The fundamental source is vast and open, devoid of forms such as self and other, love and hate, gain and loss, or coming and going. As it is said:
Spontaneous and effortless, like a simpleton; naturally, there is one who understands and loves this within their own house.

To Lady Zhang, I show this great causal nexus, which is a special practice and a unique proclamation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, intended to receive those of the highest vehicle and sharp faculties.
A person of keen faculties must transcend emotions and leave behind views to awaken to the pivotal mechanism. They must pass through with a vivid, independent clarity;
they are already familiar before a movement occurs and have already grasped it before a word is spoken. As soon as there is even a trace of a sign, they cut it off completely.

Directly beneath them, they acknowledge nothing else; they never seek or ponder within the roots of conceptual thought. One must rouse one's spirit and take full responsibility in the presence of reality, just as [the ancients did].

The sun-disk in the great void illuminates nothing it does not reach; therefore, since ancient times, the virtuous ones have reached the point of single-minded focus where not even a hair’s breadth can be manipulated or shifted.

This makes one pure and naked, bright and clear—unpartnered with the myriad dharmas and sharing no common dwelling with the thousand sages—transcending alone and ascending freely and at ease. For this reason, Deshan and Linji...

The staff and the shout fly back and forth; appearing and disappearing, releasing and seizing, they do not abide within fixed patterns. As for the verbal mechanisms and applications, they are suddenly cut off at once.
The paths of sage and ordinary are severed, and the sentiments of gain and loss are cast aside. Upon reaching the field of great rest, what more could be called birth and death?
Within the breast, things are taken with ease; even illumination does not stand. Meeting conditions, one immediately embodies the source; when brought forth, it covers heaven.
This covers the ground. Relying on the skillful means of compassion, we deliberate in the weeds;

the very purpose is to cause those of sharp faculties to cast away delusive conditions and evil perceptions, penetrating to the place of ultimate emptiness where even "emptiness" does not remain. When the mind is like the vast void, the myriad phenomena of the universe are entirely contained within it.
Thus, every single thing is sealed with certainty, attaining great liberation in every situation; this is what is called "bringing matters to completion."

Such a person has not yet even begun to practice the upward path. As for the upward practice—the place where the thousand sages have transmitted it in secret—it is not merely a wall standing ten thousand fathoms high, separated by thousands and tens of thousands of miles; even if one were to pick up the entire great earth, there would not be so much as a single speck of dust.
This is called "the Great Function Manifesting Before One. After twenty or thirty years of nurturing and maturing this, one then—
This is the realization.
"Mind itself is Buddha" is already an eight-character opening; "neither mind nor Buddha" further points it out directly before one's eyes.
If you do not seek its words but pass straight through, only then will you see the ancient’s sincere heart laid bare, slice by slice. If you hesitate, however...
You have missed it right before your face!
Who is it that does not take companionship with the myriad dharmas? I will tell you once you have swallowed up all the waters of the West River in a single gulp.
How direct and concise this is! Why do you not simply accept it as such? Do not enter further into its traces.

Within the realm of language, one will never achieve liberation. I have often seen scholars merely engage in intellectual speculation when responding to questions, seeking only to hit upon the "correct" phrasing.
How could this possibly be an insight that penetrates birth and death? To penetrate birth and death, nothing short of the awakening of the mind-ground will suffice.
This koan is the very key to unlocking the ground of the mind. It requires only that one clearly comprehend the intent beyond words;
only then will one arrive at the state free from doubt.
In the past, when Xiu Shan was seeking to see Dizang, he personally declared, "I have come this time specifically to see the Master.
I have traversed many mountains and rivers, which has been extremely arduous. Dizang pointed and said, "These many mountains and rivers are not bad for you either.
At that, [Xiu Shan] was like one whose bottom has fallen out from under his bucket; how could such a thing require many words? Even while on the road, one must maintain constant care.
Only then was it attained.

He showed Zhang Zigu that the Great Way has no fixed direction; it is simply that those of sharp faculties and noble nature awaken to a thousand truths upon hearing them once, arising neither from without nor from within.
Internally attained, it is a state of liberation like ice melting in hot water, where from the outset there is neither gain nor loss.
This is because prior to the differentiation of birth and Buddhahood, one was vast, penetrating, luminous, and wondrous, utterly without dependence, standing alone and prominent.
Yet, by following conditions with a single thought and turning one's back on this true essence, one gives rise to such incongruous activities; they flicker and drift about without a moment’s rest.
Having become habituated to grasping at objects, the source of the mind has grown turbid; this has become their constant practice.

What they see and hear never transcends sound and form, as they bind themselves solely through delusion and ignorance. When it comes to investigating the Great Liberation, it is vast and boundless, with no known limits.
The waves of consciousness surge on and on, never pausing for a moment; thus, there is no way to enter [the state].

Yet, one may possess the lingering influence of past cultivation—fragments of wholesome merit, joy, and sincere faith—and seek their source, which is indeed the supreme goodness. Upon arriving and humbly inquiring with devotion, however, one encounters only a vast, dark expanse.
This is for no other reason than that one has long since abandoned it; because it was not sustained through long-term refinement, it has become thus. Now, if you wish to...
Accept it directly and straightforwardly. Simply prepare your body and mind; silently strike at the stillness until the mental machinations are lost, becoming just like earth or wood.

Wait for the proper moment to arrive, when you will spontaneously "fall through the bottom of the bucket" and realize this original radiance—this profound, limpid, and transparent nature that is unchanging, unmoving, pure, non-active, wondrously pure, and luminous. Thus, you shall firmly establish your foundation and take deep root.
Upon reaching the adamantine, solid, true essence, one is able to carry the entire body forward in practice.
Only then can the myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences all return to a single consistency. Movement and stillness are as one; mind and object are in perfect accord.
Then, with the illumination of one, all are illuminated; with the realization of one, all are realized. Whether one lifts up Mount Sumeru or speaks of the cypress tree in the courtyard—all is so.

How could the karmic conditions and objects arise from another? As for the striking with the staff, the shouting of "Ho!", the brandishing of fists, and the rolling of the ball—each and every one was decisively sealed.
Birth and death, as well as nirvana, were like a dream from yesterday; naturally settled in great concentration and at ease, one attains the place of rest.
What more is there to doubt? Use what you need and speak what you need to say. When encountering rice, eat rice; when encountering tea, drink tea.
Accord with the ordinary mind, and do not give rise to views of Buddha or views of Dharma.

If even views of Buddha and Dharma do not arise, how much less would one give rise to a mind that creates karma or harbor unwholesome intentions? One never adopts such an attitude as to deny cause and effect. For this reason...
To attain the state of sitting and donning the robe, to practice self-discipline and subdue the mind, and to be in accord with the no-mind—this is the ultimate ground of realization.
Yongjia said: "Simply untie the soiled garment from within your own breast. Yantou said: "Merely maintain the state of quiet stillness. Yunju said:
"Among a multitude of thousands, be like one who is not there at all. Caoshan said: "It is like having passed through a place infected by a venomous spirit."
It is like water in one's own village; not even a single drop may be allowed to stain it. This is called "nurturing the holy embryo.
To be defiled is strictly forbidden. You must simply let go of all previous intellectual interpretations and the dualistic images of purity and impurity.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, investigate with your whole heart; this is the power inherent within yourself, not something bestowed by another.
It is the shortcut of the ancient virtuous ones.

This reveals the great causal conditions between the Buddhas and patriarchs for the sake of the original guest. It is not something to be understood through names, words, knowledge, views, or intellectual paths, nor is it to be grasped through cleverness or discursive thought.

One must forget the mind and forget conditions; externally empty all appearances and internally liberate oneself from consciousness and emotion, withdrawing to abide in pure emptiness and tranquility.

Tranquil, clear, and penetrating, it is luminously transcendent of all expedient means. It directly penetrates the wondrous mind of original nature, remaining profoundly still and unmoving from antiquity to the present.
Ten thousand years are but a single thought; a single thought is ten thousand years. It is the ground of eternal non-leakage and ultimate correctness.
Once attained, it is forever attained, with no possibility of change or variation. This is what is called "Directly Pointing at the Human Mind to See Nature and Attain Buddhahood. However, this...
What has been explained above is still merely theoretical discourse; it uses words to dispel words and principles to harmonize with principles, leading people gradually toward the goal.
From the outset, these were the winding paths for entering the truth—verbose and pedantic arguments that involve wading through mud and water.

Once one reaches the actual, direct extraction of the essence, how could there be such elaborate circumlocution? Therefore, when the Buddha held up a flower on Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa alone smiled. This is...

Within this, how could there be room for even a hair’s breadth of conceptual reasoning? One must penetrate to the very top and bottom, passing through the entire ocean of lands of the great thousandfold world-system in a single stroke, knowing exactly where everything falls.
Only then will one truly understand the authentic command practiced by those who have come before.
Are the staff of Deshan and the shout of Linji mere child’s play? If you possess the skillful means of a true master of the fundamental division, there is no need [for further elaboration].
A Note: This is why the Elder Pang asked Shitou, "What kind of person is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as companions?
Shitou covered his mouth, while Master Mazu said, "Wait until you can swallow all the waters of the West River in a single gulp, and then I will tell you.
Are these two ends not one? To investigate their ultimate intent, they are identical in entering the mud and entering the water; how can one hold them in high esteem [as being different]?

Distinguish between the shallow and the deep. Upon reaching this point, you must certainly realize that there is something more; once you know there is more, you must further advance before you can succeed.

Most crucially, avoid clinging to dead words and falling into conceptual traps. As soon as there is even a hair’s breadth of dualistic activity—whether in function, in the mysterious and wondrous nature of reality, or in views—it will prick and irritate you.
Unless you can suddenly strip these away, how will you penetrate and transcend birth and death to realize peace?

Delight in departing for the realm of non-action and immovability. The ancients valued the practice of entering through a single gate; once having attained this, they would sit, put on their robes, and look back at themselves—this is precisely it.
You must certainly maintain and sustain this practice so that you gain its power; only then will it be excellent.
The ancient sages and worthies possessed great capacity; they were able both to realize it for themselves and to put it into practice—this is called "the two acts.
For a long time, one should simply observe one's own arising thoughts and mental stirrings; as soon as even a hair’s breadth appears, one must immediately cause it to be purified and exhausted.

Ultimately, one must not engage in any worldly activity, nor seek to provide material support for the sake of conversation, nor hope to surpass others by suppressing their insights, nor strive to create superior schemes for the sake of fame and reputation.
In truth, one’s sole purpose should be the great matter of birth and death, so that through hundreds and thousands of kalpas and lifetimes, one remains undeluded and does not fall into ruin.
Since ancient times, there have been many who, without sparing even their own eyebrows, have pointed out the way for others. — Yunmen.
To encounter the essence directly is to realize the absolute truth. Linji sat and cut off the heads of both the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas.
Deshan had no concerns in his mind; when the mind has no concerns, it is empty yet spiritual, still yet illuminating. Yantou simply maintained a state of leisurely ease;
at all times, being without desire and without dependence, he naturally transcended all *samādhis*. Zhaozhou said, "I have seen hundreds of thousands of men."
One merely seeks those who would become Buddhas; among them, it is difficult to find a person of no-mind.
Simply savor these words deeply, let the mind rest, and practice accordingly. At some future time, when you encounter circumstances and conditions, you will gain power.
You must be careful to guard this and not allow it to leak away; this is the secret instruction.
When Prime Minister Pei saw that Huangbo had attained realization upon hearing his words, he further elucidated the secret essentials for transmitting the mind.
He exhorted him repeatedly with boundless compassion. Yu Di of Xiangyang went to visit Ziyu; at the first call, he turned his head back.

I shall once again point this out for you: it was only when one saw the ship tossed by black winds and about to fall into the land of the rākṣasas that one could finally attain a state of profound clarity.

Since antiquity, how many among the ranks of scholars have been willing to value this matter so highly as to neglect sleep and forget their meals? Those who have directly perceived the Truth are beyond counting;

all of them did so because their own faculties, powers, wisdom, and insight were lofty, brilliant, and sharp, enabling them thereafter to seek out and resolve the truth. Now, since [you] are compared to those of antiquity...
Fellow practitioners, you should especially exert yourselves with non-retrogression, striving for profound realization and deep penetration. Do not merely value verbal expressions;
you must ensure that mind after mind does not touch external objects and that, at every turn, there is no fixed locus. Only then will it be attained.
This path values single-minded extraction and solitary realization; it accords with the upward-turning pivot of the patriarchs and Buddhas.

It rises far above the source of the mind like the flash of sparks from striking stone or a bolt of lightning—admitting no room for deliberation or discursive thought. One must penetrate directly, without falling into the roots of consciousness or the realms of conceptual emotion.
This extends even to the explanation of principles and nature, which must not be used as a nest or a basis for establishing intellectual understanding within the context of words and phrases.

Passing it down and holding it in turn, they preach "Mind-Only," merging earth, water, fire, and wind with space as their measure, calling this the matter of "penetrating the sense-faculties and objects.

Yet this merely establishes a theoretical system that does not transcend the three vehicles and five natures of the doctrinal schools; the provisional setting up of stages only results in a state of stagnation.
One must truly realize that before there were Buddhas or patriarchs, from what did that single fragment of ground arise?
Where does it come from? To have even the slightest trace of attainment is merely semblance-prajñā. You must discern this deeply and not fall into the trap of worldly mechanisms.
When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, if you lack clarity in the ground of principle and cannot decisively sever [delusions], at that time you will be terrified and bewildered;
regret will be of no avail. Master Wuzu often instructed his disciples: "You must investigate when facing the end of life."

The meditation at the time of death is no small matter. Even if one possesses cleverness, eloquence, and the eight penetrations or seven masteries, engaging in subtle or grand theoretical discourse—drawing out threads and following lines—is nothing more than analyzing antiquities; it ultimately provides no point of severance.
Therefore, from ancient times, great virtuous ones and eminent masters of the Way have possessed extraordinary faculties and superior intelligence.
